World.title: Olivia Dunne fires back at MLB team over obnoxious comment, NFL WAG Gia Duddy sizzles & ESPN's bloodbath
World.content:
Penultimate Hump Day of July AND we have NFL teams reporting for training camp today? How lucky are we?

It's all coming together, folks. I can smell it. We're grinding right now, but it's close to paying off. August begins next week. This Saturday marks the five-week countdown to our first college football game of the year.

Five weeks. I've got cartons of milk in the fridge older than that. Who has it better than us, boys and girls? Nobody.

Let's roll.

Welcome to a Hump Day Nightcaps — the one where Olivia Dunne tells the Cleveland Indians (yep) to kick rocks while Paul Skenes stuffs them in a locker.

What else? I've got plenty of fallout from ESPN's ... rough ... week, Gia Duddy checks in, and Charlie Woods is sounding more and more like his daddy on the course.

That's a good thing, by the way. Always a good thing to be like Tiger on the course. Not so much off of it.

Grab you a brick wall to run through after you hear this speech from John Harbaugh, and settle in for a Hump Day 'Cap!

Olivia Dunne stands by her man

Lordy, John. What was that? To be fair, Harbaugh hasn't really had to do an introductory speech in two decades, so he's understandably rusty.

But goodness ... give me something. Anything. Let's get these fellas fired up, coach! Football is back. That's the worst thing I had to sit through today, and I had an hour Zoom call on "content creation."

Oh well. Harbaugh and the Giants will be a story all year. Can't wait to see that team on the field.

But first, let's head out to the diamond with Olivia Dunne and the Pittsburgh Pirates, and get this call started.

For those who weren't locked in on this week's thrilling Pirates-Guardians game, Paul Skenes dominated over 7 innings, giving up one run and striking out 8 in a 7-1 win.

Some poor intern who runs Cleveland's account jumped the gun when the game was tied 1-1, calling out Livvy with a slick little caption.

Our girl made sure to fire back:

This Pat McAfee narrative is silly

"Game was Dunne at 7-1 Pirates."

Don't come at MLB's First Lady and miss, Indians! Paul Skenes, by the way, appears to have his swagger back. After a rocky start to the summer, he's given up just five runs over his last three starts (3-0) and stuck out 19.

The "Paul Skenes has lost his stuff" narrative appears to have been greatly exaggerated. Weird how those things happen, right?

Speaking of narratives ... let's talk about this Pat McAfee nonsense that's starting to percolate in the wake of ESPN's summer housecleaning.

For those who missed it (don't know how that's possible if you read OutKick/Fox News), the World Wide (Woke) Leader laid off (fired) dozens of employees yesterday.

Ryan Clark was let go during NFL Live. Cam Newton was canned. Tom Pelissero was cut. It was a gutting.

Pat McAfee, meanwhile, is reportedly earning close to $30 million and in talks to double that salary pretty soon.

JJ Watt joined the "progrum" yesterday and ... addressed the elephant in the room:

Charlie, Karl & Gia, oh my!

"Slow, slow news day over there on the ESPN airwaves, huh?" Watt said to begin the interview. "I mean, besides the fact that you’re getting $100 million… Did they keep anybody? Or is everybody fired to pay you? I’m trying to figure that out."

This narrative that ESPN fired all these guys to pay McAfee is so stupid. The narrative that Pat McAfee's salary is ultimately what got Ryan Clark fired is even dumber.

Here's the bottom line: ESPN views Pat McAfee as an asset. The network has put him everywhere since the two partnered up a few years back. Everywhere. Not just football, either.

He was just at the Home Run Derby last week! An event, by the way, that wasn't on ESPN for the first time in three decades.

Pat McAfee didn't cost Ryan Clark his job. Ryan Clark lost his job because he brought nothing to the table for ESPN, beyond an (increasingly) occasional headache because he said something stupid.

ESPN chose to cut ties with a liability, and put more money into an asset. That's not a new or novel concept.

It's how businesses have been run for years.

OK, let's rapid-fire this Hump Day class into a big Hump Day night. First up? You know who ESPN absolutely should NOT have fired?

Karl Ravech.

Remember the old days at ESPN? The glory days of baseball when they had Ravech, Peter Gammons and Harold Reynolds on set? Mix in some John Kruk and Steve Phillips, and boy, was it an absolute party.

Now? ESPN doesn't care about baseball. They've decided to put all their eggs in the NBA basket, and continue to distance themselves from baseball. The firing of Karl Ravech — who'd been there for 33 (!!!) years — was disgusting.

But not surprising.

Next? You know what else is disgusting? This little moment from Charlie Woods' round earlier this week:

Taking a picture during someone's backswing — a kid's backswing — during a golf tournament is just the worst. God, these people are insufferable.

Personally, I think every golf course in America should adopt Augusta's no cellphone policy. I'm serious. It's, easily, the best rule in sports.

PS: How about the absolute disgust out from Charlie after that iron off the tee? Reminds me of this great Tiger moment from back in the day:

Man, I miss the Big Cat on the course. We had it so good.

OK, that's it for today. Good work, everyone. In honor of NFL camps officially opening today, here's infamous NFL Draft WAG Gia Duddy begging summer to stick around just a few weeks longer.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

See you tomorrow.

Is McAfee to blame for Ryan Clark's firing? Email me at Zach.Dean@OutKick.com.

World.title: Trump attends dignified transfer of 4 service members killed in Iran attacks since the ceasefire ended
World.content:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday attended the dignified transfer of the remains of four service members killed in Iranian attacks this month after hostilities ramped up following the collapse of the ceasefire.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

The four service members being flown from the Middle East to Dover Air Force Base were 28-year-old Angel S. Rampersad of New York, 30-year-old Michael Emmanuel Swinton of North Carolina, 25-year-old Tyler James Feehan of Hawaii and 19-year-old Isabella Gonzales of Texas.

Dignified transfers are some of the most solemn occasions for presidents, who often attend to pay respects to troops killed in conflicts overseen by them as commander in chief. Trump has attended two prior dignified transfers since the war began in February, but this is his first since he declared on July 8 that the ceasefire was over.

President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth salute as members of a U.S. Army carry team move a transfer case Wednesday. Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images

The event marked the latest impact of the war, which has garnered criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle who question the administration’s strategy in the monthslong conflict. The hostilities, which were paused after the two sides agreed to a peace plan that quickly fell apart, have thrown the region into chaos, leaving at least 18 Americans dead, costing at least $37.5 billion and inflating the price of oil.

The president and his administration have vigorously defended their handling of the war, arguing it is necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

Trump told reporters earlier Wednesday: “We’re going to Dover. Some of you are going with us. To honor our heroes, and they are indeed great heroes, actually. They said, and all of them said very strongly, we can’t let, we cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon. They won’t have a nuclear weapon. So we’re going to honor them. And it’s one of the hardest things to do, for me, it’s one of the hardest things to do as a president, but has to be done.”

The family members of the fallen service members attended the dignified transfer, where the bodies of their loved ones were moved in American flag-draped transfer cases from a plane into waiting vans.

Uniformed service members marched the transfer cases past officials, including Trump, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine and White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt. Sens. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and Chris Coons, D-Del., also attended.

Trump and other officials saluted as the remains passed before them, while others placed their hands on their hearts. The president also met privately with the families, the White House confirmed.

From left, Pvt. Isabella Gonzales; 1st Lt. Tyler James Feehan; Sgt. Angel Rampersad; Sgt. Michael Emmanuel Swinton. DVIDS

Flag-draped transfer cases are loaded into vehicles Wednesday at Dover Air Force Base. Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images

Gonzales was killed Friday and Feehan was killed Saturday, the Pentagon said. It also said that Swinton was killed Sunday “during a controlled detonation” of an attack drone.

Rampersad was “believed to have been killed” in Jordan, the Pentagon said, adding that “the incident is under investigation.” The Pentagon has said that she is believed to have been the missing soldier who is presumed dead.

Hegseth faced questions from senators Tuesday about the cost and strategy of the war during a tense hearing on the Pentagon’s budget request.

During one particularly heated exchange, Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., called the Trump administration’s efforts “an utter and complete failure” and pressed Hegseth on what the long-term plan is to end the war.

“You have over a trillion dollars,” Peters said. “You’re asking for one and a half trillion dollars. It’s not a question of money. It’s a question of leadership and understanding what it takes to actually win.”

World.title: Trump approves landmark U.S.-Saudi nuclear deal
World.content:
President Donald Trump has approved a landmark civilian nuclear deal between the United States and Saudi Arabia that is expected to be announced Wednesday, a senior administration official told NBC News.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

The agreement will see the U.S. support the creation of a nuclear power program and see American companies build the program in the kingdom, said the official who was granted anonymity by NBC News so that the person could speak about the deal before its official announcement.

News of the agreement was first reported in The Wall Street Journal.

Congress will be required to vote on the agreement, but would need a veto-proof majority to actually block the deal, which could pave the way for the kingdom to pursue its own uranium enrichment and likely raise fears of nuclear proliferation.

Asked ahead of the announcement about those concerns and reports of an expected deal, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that the U.S. would not “reach any agreement with any country in the world that leads to the risk of proliferation.”

The agreement comes as the war against Iran that was launched by the U.S. and Israel in late February goes on. Trump has insisted that Tehran should not be able to develop a nuclear weapon, despite the Islamic Republic consistently denying that it plans to do so.

An agreement to normalize ties between Israel and Saudi Arabia had previously been a U.S. requirement for any deal allowing the kingdom to enrich uranium, but Saudi leaders insisted this would not be possible without meaningful progress toward a Palestinian state.

However, Energy Secretary Chris Wright discussed building the country’s commercial nuclear power industry with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, on a visit to the kingdom last year, shortly before Trump traveled there himself in May 2025.

Any deal without appropriate guardrails in place would be “concerning from a proliferation perspective,” according to Darya Dolzikova​, a senior research fellow with the proliferation and nuclear policy program at the Royal United Services Institute, a London-based think tank.

“Any country, period, but particularly countries of proliferation concern have to be really, really robust on their nonproliferation provisions,” she added.

And Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has previously warned that the kingdom would try to obtain a nuclear weapon if Iran was also able to do, Dolzikova​ noted.

Saudi Arabia also signed a mutual defense pact with Pakistan, the only Muslim nuclear nation, in September. Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Asif then said his nation’s nuclear program would “be made available” to Saudi Arabia if required.

The Middle Eastern kingdom is a member state of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which promotes peaceful nuclear work but also inspects nations to ensure they don’t have clandestine atomic weapon programs. Based in Vienna, the agency reports to the United Nations General Assembly and Security Council.

While enrichment does not necessarily lead to a nuclear weapon, it can open the door to it. However, any country wishing to do so would also have to master other technologies including the use of synchronized high explosives.

And there has been focus on whether any deal would include the “gold standard” safeguards that would block the kingdom from enriching uranium and reprocessing spent nuclear fuel, both of which are potential pathways to nuclear weapons.

It also remains to be seen whether the agreement includes the “Additional Protocol” that grants the IAEA greater oversight of a country’s nuclear activities.

Ultimately, “the devil will be in the details,” Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East and North Africa program at the London-based think tank Chatham House, said. If Saudi Arabia does retain the right to enrich, she said, “it’s the issue of domestic enrichment that will be more concerning and alarming.”

The deal with the U.S. came a day after senior Saudi and United Arab Emirates officials shared similar social media posts ​affirming their close historical ties and “wise leadership,” a move that follows months of tensions owing to a rift ‌between the two Gulf monarchies.

The Gulf nations have been split over ​their support for opposing sides in the war in Yemen that culminated in a Saudi airstrike late last year, on what it said was a shipment of UAE military equipment to the Yemeni faction Abu Dhabi backed.

Their interests have diverged over a number of issues including oil quotas.

But the posts from the Saudi Minister of Media Salman Al-Dosary and Abdulla bin Mohamed Alhamed, Chairman of the UAE National Media Authority, said they should focus on their shared history and heritage.

World.title: Oil surges past $95 as U.S. downplays Iran diplomacy and 2nd key trade route is disrupted
World.content:
The price of oil surged nearly 5% Wednesday as U.S. officials talked down the chance of new peace talks after an 11th straight night of strikes on Iran and with major disruption now facing two of the world’s key supply routes.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

International Brent crude oil rose as much as 4.9% to more than $95 per barrel for the first time in almost six weeks. U.S. crude oil rose as much as nearly 5.1% to nearly $89 per barrel.

Those prices pulled back slightly after stocks opened at 9:30 a.m. ET. Both benchmarks were still higher by more than 3%.

While Brent is widely considered the international oil benchmark, it also influences the retail cost of gas in the U.S.

Those pump prices rose again Wednesday, extending their climb above $4 per gallon. The national average price rose 4 cents overnight to $4.06 per gallon, according to motor club AAA data tracked by NBC News.

Treasury yields spiked, following oil’s latest jump and it’s likely impact on inflation. As of mid-morning trading, the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield was hovering around 4.65%, its highest since May.

As a result, the average rate on a 30-year mortgage rose to 6.75% Wednesday, matching its highest level of the year.

Since the start of the month, oil prices have gained 30% and are now up more than 55% since the start of the year. That move has largely erased the drop in prices that came after the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June.

Rhetoric escalates tensions

President Donald Trump had declared that tentative deal, which was aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, “over” on July 8.

But on Wednesday, Trump ratcheted up the rhetoric once again.

“Any time the Islamic Republic of Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, whether it be by Missile, Rocket, Drone, or any other device or weapon, the United States will bomb and destroy ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT, including those located next to, or in, the Capital City of Tehran,” he posted on social media.

Overnight, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the U.S. remained open to diplomacy with Iran, “but right now they don’t seem to be serious about that.”

Rubio added that the U.S. would continue to try to protect commercial shipping.

But in the last two days, the U.K.’s Maritime Trade Organization has reported multiple attacks on vessels in the area. In at least two of those, the maritime monitoring group that is aligned with the British navy said that crews were forced to abandon ship.

Those attacks are one reason why traffic in the Strait of Hormuz remains extremely low.

On Monday, only 13 ships crossed the vital waterway and on Tuesday that number was only 9, according to an analysis of ship movements by MarineTraffic.

World.title: Trump-backed Rep. Andy Biggs wins GOP primary for Arizona governor
World.content:
Rep. Andy Biggs has won the Republican primary in Arizona’s race for governor, NBC News projects, setting up a battleground state matchup this fall with Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

Biggs, a former chair of the conservative House Freedom Caucus who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, emerged from a primary field that included fellow Rep. David Schweikert and businessmen Scott Neely and Ken Miceli.

Biggs, who has represented a district outside Phoenix for five terms and held a consistent lead in the polls leading up to the primary, continually leaned into Trump’s backing in his campaign and highlighted his support for border security and lowering taxes.

But the Trump dynamic could play differently in the general election in Arizona, one of five states Trump won in 2024 where a Democratic-controlled governorship is on the ballot in 2026.

Democrats have found success in Arizona, once a traditional Republican stronghold, running against Trump-aligned candidates in recent cycles. In addition to a Democratic governor, Arizona is represented by two Democratic U.S. senators, and the party controls the secretary of state and attorney general offices.

In the final stretch of the primary, Biggs sought to cast himself as someone who has worked across the political aisle in Congress, an apparent effort to appeal to the state’s huge chunk of independent voters. More than one-third of the state’s voters are not registered with either major political party.

“I may be conservative, but I’ve also shown that even when you’re conservative, if you look to collaborate, you can find points and ways to collaborate with even people who fundamentally disagree with you on other things,” Biggs told USA Today on Sunday.

Gov. Katie Hobbs is running for a second term this fall. Megan Mendoza / The Republic / USA Today Network via Reuters file

Biggs had long questioned the legitimacy of Joe Biden’s victory in the 2020 presidential election. In his recent USA Today interview, he dodged questions about that outcome, saying, “I’m not going to be critical against Republicans, and we have a lot of people with a lot of diverse viewpoints.” He added that Republicans will win “by looking forward and having a vision for the state.”

Meanwhile, Hobbs, who won her 2022 election by less than 1 percentage point, ran unopposed in Tuesday’s Democratic primary. With the national political environment expected to favor Democrats, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter this month shifted its rating of the Arizona governor’s race from “toss-up” to “lean Democrat.”

World.title: Democratic leaders’ pick trails in Arizona primary for a key battleground district
World.content:
Democrat Amish Shah, a physician and former state lawmaker, has opened a lead in the primary for a key Arizona battleground district despite party leaders backing another candidate.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

NBC News has not yet projected a winner in the 1st District Democratic primary, but Shah’s 7-point edge with 84% of the expected vote counted comes despite an onslaught of late ads attacking him and boosting his opponent, Democrat Marlene Galán-Woods, a former journalist backed by Democratic leaders in Arizona and Washington, D.C. That includes the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which waded in for Galán-Woods.

Shah was the Democratic nominee in 2024 and narrowly lost that year to GOP Rep. David Schweikert, who ran for governor but lost the Republican primary Tuesday night.

This year, the 1st District Democratic nominee will face off against Republican Jay Feely, the former professional football kicker who won his primary in the district Tuesday thanks in part to the blessing of President Donald Trump. Trump carried the district by 3 points in 2024.

Jay Feely outside a polling location in Fountain Hills, Ariz., on Tuesday. Cassidy Araiza / Bloomberg via Getty Images

“This seat is such an important seat,” Feely said at an election night event. “You know how close the House is, and there’s three to five seats in the country that will determine who holds the House and who controls the House in November. This is one of those seats.”

Shah’s 2026 campaign leaned heavily on his legislative record, arguing he pushed back against Republicans and the Trump administration in Arizona and would do so again in Washington. He also emphasized his work as an emergency room doctor, campaigning on healthcare issues and abortion access.

Millions of dollars in outside money flooded into the Democratic primary for the Maricopa County-based seat in the final weeks, funding ads attacking Shah over his voting record in the state Legislature and saying he has aligned with conservatives on hot-button social issues.

The DCCC joined in too, a relatively uncommon move from the House Democratic campaign arm, which has only spent campaign cash in a handful of competitive Democratic primaries over the years. The group’s ads alongside Galán-Woods emphasized her endorsement from Arizona Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly.

Shah fought back against the outside group attack ads, lamenting how “dark money groups are attacking me, trying to scam [voters] with deliberate disinformation” about his voting record. He also pushed back vocally against national Democrats putting their thumb on the scale, attacking the “broken cabal” in an interview with The New York Times.

If Shah wins the nomination, it would be the third time this election cycle that a DCCC-backed candidate lost a primary, following battleground district primaries in Maine and California.

On the Republican side, Feely’s fame and support from Trump instantly made him the heavy favorite in his party’s primary. Feely initially launched a campaign for Arizona’s 5th District — a deep red seat left open by Republican Rep. Andy Biggs’ run for governor — but later decided to run here instead.

He’s leaned heavily on his endorsement from Trump, seeking to tie would-be Democratic opponents to the most liberal wing of their party and blaming inflation and the rise of housing on Democrats. Democrats are almost certain to do the reverse, tying Feely to Trump in the hopes of hurting his image with swing voters. Moderates in Arizona have broken against Trump-backed candidates in recent elections, though Trump carried the state in 2024.

Rep. Juan Ciscomani, R-Ariz., at the Capitol Hill Club in Washington on May 13. Bill Clark / CQ-Roll Call via Getty Images file

There wasn’t any suspense in Arizona’s other major House battleground, the 6th District in the southeastern part of the state. There, Republican Rep. Juan Ciscomani is running against Democrat JoAnna Mendoza, a Marine veteran who later worked as a congressional and political aide.

There was a similar lack of suspense in the 2nd District, a red district Trump won by 15 points in 2024. There, Democrats nominated former Navajo Nation President Jonathan Nez to take on Republican Rep. Eli Crane, a rematch after Crane beat Nez by 9 points two years ago.

Another Trump-endorsed candidate won his primary for Biggs’ open seat Tuesday. Former Pinal County Sheriff Mark Lamb will be the heavy favorite to win this suburban Phoenix seat Trump won by 20 points in 2024.

Despite Trump’s backing, Lamb faced criticism after an Arizona Republican investigation found that his church investigated allegations of sexual impropriety against him. Lamb denies the allegations, and the Pinal County attorney’s office closed an investigation, finding “no abuse of power or criminal violation.”

World.title: Alexander Kolodin, who tried to overturn Arizona election results, wins GOP nod for secretary of state
World.content:
Republican state Rep. Alexander Kolodin will face Arizona’s Democratic secretary of state, Adrian Fontes, in November’s general election, NBC News projects, after he won the GOP primary.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

Kolodin won the Republican nomination over former state GOP chair Gina Swoboda.

Kolodin, who has frequently questioned the results of past elections in interviews, led several lawsuits to overturn the results of the 2020 and 2022 elections in Arizona, earning rebukes from judges and the state bar association. Kolodin is backed by the conservative nonprofit group Turning Point USA and several Arizona GOP members of Congress.

Now, he’s running to be the chief election officer in a battleground state during the 2028 presidential campaign. Part of the role of secretary of state in Arizona is overseeing state elections. The office’s duties include working to certify “voting devices, election results, candidates and measures to the ballot, as well as the results of statewide elections,” according to the secretary of state’s website.

In a joint PBS interview featuring the two candidates, Kolodin said Arizona voters are looking for more transparency and openness in their elections.

“They are not getting that from Adrian Fontes; they will get that from me,” Kolodin said.

“I think voters in this primary and across this state have serious concerns with the way their elections are being administered,” he said. Kolodin also said people in the state can never be confident in their elections without more observers at polling stations.

Fontes, who previously ran elections in Maricopa County, Arizona’s largest county, has been outspoken about President Donald Trump and allies’ efforts to cast doubt on election results in Arizona and elsewhere. He defeated a Trump-endorsed Republican opponent in 2022 and is seeking a second term.

Fontes administered the election in Arizona in 2024, when Trump carried the state and won his second term as president. Trump narrowly lost Arizona in 2020.

World.title: What to know about Taylor Farms amid the cyclospora outbreak
World.content:
Produce giant Taylor Farms is under renewed scrutiny after it voluntarily recalled iceberg lettuce linked to the nation's unusually large cyclosporiasis outbreak.

Food safety experts say that while recalls are inevitable for a produce supplier the size of Taylor Farms, the current outbreak is unusual because of its scale and the number of people sickened.

More than 5,000 cases of cyclosporiasis have been reported, far exceeding the typical annual level of roughly 200 to 1,000 cases. Because cyclospora infections can cause severe diarrhea lasting days or even weeks, some consumers are avoiding leafy greens and other fresh produce commonly associated with the parasite while investigators search for the source.

"Nothing about this outbreak is typical," Jennifer McEntire, founder of food safety consulting firm Food Safety Strategy, told CBS News. "When you see something of this magnitude, it's surprising, even to those of us who are accustomed to working with outbreaks. This is not normal, and it's not acceptable."

Taylor Farms did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.

How big is Taylor Farms?

Taylor Farms, founded by CEO Bruce Taylor in 1995 in Salinas Valley, California, manages a network of dozens of production facilities in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, and Western Europe. It grows one-quarter of its own produce and partners with family-owned farms to supply the rest, the company said in its 2025 impact report.

The company, which employs 25,000 people, booked $6 billion in revenue in 2022, according to the most recent data available, ranking it among the largest produce suppliers in the U.S.

Its sheer size positions it as a key supplier of lettuce and other produce to the nation's biggest retailers, including Walmart, Costco, Target and Whole Foods, and restaurant chains Taco Bell and McDonald's. The company also owns the organic brand Earthbound Farms, and produces 40% of the salad kits sold in the U.S.

Consumers may mistake Taylor Farms for a small single-farm operation based on its name alone, McEntire said. "But it's not. It's an enormous company with multiple processing operations and growing locations in different regions," she said.

What's known about Taylor Farms' iceberg lettuce?

On July 17, Taylor Farms voluntarily recalled potentially affected iceberg lettuce from central Mexico, after federal investigators established a link between lettuce served at some Taco Bell restaurants and Taylor Farms de Mexico. The company's other products, including its salad kits, have not been recalled.

The company said that the FDA had identified a single independent farm, accounting for less than 1% of the U.S.'s iceberg lettuce supply, as the potential source of the outbreak.

On Sunday, the FDA backtracked, saying that a test that showed contaminated iceberg lettuce was a false positive. In response, Taylor Farms issued a statement saying the agency "apologized to us."

On Monday, however, the FDA said that the "false-positive lab sample DOES NOT change the basis for [the] FDA's ongoing outbreak investigation or the overwhelming epidemiological data supporting the current voluntary recall by Taylor Farms." The agency added that its "traceback investigation and outbreak data continue to converge on shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms locations in central Mexico."

The false positive "doesn't call into question the conclusion of the outbreak investigation," McEntire said. Had the positive test been confirmed, "it could've resulted in a substantially expanded recall."

CBS News medical correspondent Dr. Céline Gounder said that while it's rare for the FDA to publicly walk back test results, such false positives are "ordinary as a laboratory event." Testing for the cyclospora parasite is also more complicated than for other pathogens, such as E. coli or Salmonella, McEntire said.

"The unusual thing isn't the false positive. It's that an unconfirmed single-sample result went public on a Saturday and was withdrawn on a Sunday," Dr. Gounder said. "The question I'd ask FDA is not 'how did the lab get it wrong' but 'what is your policy for announcing a presumptive positive before confirmatory testing closes, and did you follow it?'"

The FDA did not immediately respond to CBS News' inquiry about the state of the investigation, or immediately indicate what its protocol is for announcing test results.

What is Taylor Farms' history of food safety?

Taylor Farms has been connected to several previous food safety investigations and recalls.

In 2024, Taylor Farms supplied slivered onions served on McDonald's Quarter Pounders that were contaminated with E. coli, leading to one death and more than 100 illnesses, according to the FDA. The FDA found dozens of violations at a Taylor Farms facility that supplied the onions, including dirty equipment.

In 2020, Taylor Farms recalled several products containing onions from a third-party supplier due to concerns that they could be contaminated with Salmonella.

In 2013, Taylor Farms' salad mixes produced in Guanajuato, Mexico, and supplied to Olive Garden and Red Lobster restaurants were also linked to a Cyclospora outbreak in 2013, which led to hundreds of illnesses across the U.S, according to the CDC.

Has this impacted Taco Bell or produce sales?

Foot traffic at Taco Bell restaurants across the U.S. was down by 31% on July 17 compared to the average number of visits on a Friday for the rest of the year, according to R.J. Hottovy, head of analytical research at Placer.ai, a location analytics firm measuring foot traffic at retailers and restaurants.

Consumers reacted even before federal officials linked Taylor Farms' produce served at Taco Bell, with some consumers sharing tips about where they had eaten before falling ill with cyclosporiasis.

A brand that has suffered a food safety incident can recover from reputational damage if it's transparent with the public, experts told CBS News.

On Friday, Taco Bell preemptively removed potentially contaminated food items from its menus in certain states before any recalls had been announced.

"They got out ahead of the story. They didn't wait for the FDA or the CDC, and that's good," Sandra Eskin, the CEO of Stop Foodborne Illness and the former deputy undersecretary of food safety at the U.S. Department of Agriculture, told CBS News.

The full impact of the outbreak on the reputations of Taylor Farms, Taco Bell and other stakeholders won't be known for some time.

"There is still a lot of uncertainty, and we don't have full clarity. We will have to wait to determine just what happened and who is at fault to be able to say which brand will be hit the hardest," Hottovy said.

World.title: Taylor Farms pulls iceberg lettuce linked to cyclosporiasis outbreak
World.content:
Taylor Farms on Friday said it is "voluntarily removing" iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico after it was linked to one of the largest outbreaks of cyclosporiasis in the U.S. in recent years.

"While the FDA traceback is indicating a specific independent farm, which represents less than 1% of the U.S.'s iceberg lettuce supply, as the potential source of the outbreak, we have removed all iceberg lettuce from the region indefinitely," the company said in a statement.

The Food and Drug Administration said in a statement Friday night that its traceback investigation identified a single supplier, Taylor Farms de Mexico, and that consumers should avoid eating shredded iceberg lettuce from Mexico at Taco Bells in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and West Virginia while its investigation continues.

In a follow-up notice on Saturday, the FDA said that a sample of lettuce from Mexico that was supplied by Taylor Farms had tested positive for cyclospora, the parasite which causes cyclosporiasis.

"This sample was collected during targeted import surveillance as a result of this outbreak investigation," the FDA said in a statement, adding though that the positive sample was not part of Taylor Farms' current recall.

"They are currently working to identify whether any part of this implicated lot is available in commerce or in consumers homes," the FDA said.

On Thursday, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention identified lettuce supplied to select Taco Bell restaurants as a source of the multistate outbreak, more than a month after cases first began to appear.

A source familiar with the investigation had told CBS News on Thursday that the supplier was Salinas, California-based Taylor Farms. The iceberg lettuce was distributed to Taco Bell restaurants in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and West Virginia, according to the CDC.

The Department of Health and Human Services said the investigation is continuing.

"The investigation remains active, and additional states, restaurants, retailers, or products may be identified as more information becomes available," said Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for HHS.

Taco Bell removes lettuce

Taco Bell said that as of Friday, it "has completed removal of affected Taylor Farms lettuce from our restaurants."

"Based on ongoing conversations with public health officials, and out of an abundance of caution, Taco Bell worked swiftly to voluntarily remove the product from restaurants and the affected ingredient has been removed from our supply chain nationwide," Taco Bell Corp. said Friday in a statement. "We took this action to ensure our guests can enjoy their Taco Bell favorites safely."

"We believe public health is a shared responsibility among restaurants, their suppliers, and authorities, and we are proud to have consistently acted quickly and proactively to protect our guests," Taco Bell Corp. said. "Taco Bell has taken precautionary action, and we encourage all relevant restaurants, retailers, and foodservice operators to do the same."

Data shows that sales at the fast-food chain have taken a hit amid the outbreak. According to Consumer Edge, which compiles spending data based on credit and debit transactions, year-over-year sales growth at Taco Bell was 4.2% in the week ending July 11, the slowest rate since April.

"Our data still shows positive year-over-year sales growth for Taco Bell, but that growth has slowed very recently," Michael Gunther, senior vice president of research and market intelligence at Consumer Edge, told CBS News in an email.

Concerns about the outbreak could be the cause of the slower growth, he added.

The outbreak could also be dampening foot traffic at Taco Bell and other fast-food chains with lettuce-heavy menus, separate data from the foot traffic analytics platform Placer.ai shows.

"While we only have a few days of data to work with, cyclospora headlines and product removals at some QSR [quick service restaurant] chains appear to be weighing modestly on visitation," the analytical team for Placer.ai said in an email.

Walmart removes some lettuce products as a precaution

Retail giant Walmart announced Saturday it was also removing four Marketside bagged iceberg lettuce salad products from its stores in more than two dozen states.

"Although there is no indication that products sold in our stores are affected by the current Cyclospora investigations, we have removed four bagged iceberg lettuce salad products from select locations as a precaution after receiving notice from our supplier," Walmart said in a statement, noting that "there have been no confirmed illnesses associated with these products at this time."

The retailer advised those who have purchased the products to discard them or return them for a refund, out of an abundance of caution.

Scope of the outbreak

The outbreak, first reported in May, has spread to 34 states, sickening at least 1,644 people, according to the CDC. However, the CDC's tally lags behind state health departments, which have reported much larger numbers of cases. For instance, the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services reported more than 5,000 confirmed cases as of Friday.

No deaths have been reported.

"As a family-owned company, we are deeply concerned for those who became ill, their families, and the Americans whose trust in the safety of fresh produce has been shaken," Taylor Farms said in its statement Friday.

"We are committed to doing everything in our power to address this issue, support the ongoing investigation, and help restore trust," the company added.

What is cyclosporiasis?

The food- and waterborne illness cyclosporiasis is caused by the cyclospora parasite, which causes long-lasting, watery and sometimes explosive diarrhea, according to public health experts.

Outbreaks typically occur in the late spring and summer, and have historically been linked to bagged salads, cilantro, basil, raspberries, snow peas and green onions.

Editor's note: This story has been updated to clarify that the investigation is continuing and other sources could still be identified.

World.title: Tropical Storm Bertha makes landfall on Gulf Coast. See its path.
World.content:
Tropical Storm Bertha made landfall in St. Bernard Parish, Louisiana, Wednesday afternoon. The storm is bringing rain to a large swath of the northern Gulf Coast, with a series of watches and warnings issued along its path.

Bertha is crawling westward "with little acceleration," the National Hurricane Center said. Forecasters said the storm would move over the New Orleans area Wednesday night and continue on toward Houston before dissipating by the end of the week.

Beaches were closed from Florida to Mississippi as Bertha's tropical-storm-force winds reached more than 100 miles outward from its center.

Map shows projected path

Bertha, the second named storm of the Atlantic hurricane season, is forecast to stick close to the coast. The Miami-based hurricane center said it expects the system to continue gradually weakening as it moves along the northern Gulf Coast over the next couple of days.

As of the center's latest update Wednesday, the storm had maximum sustained winds of 45 mph, which have decreased gradually since Tuesday night.

CBS News

Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry urged residents not to be complacent about the potential flooding threat.

"It doesn't take a major hurricane to do major damage to communities in Louisiana," Landry said at a news conference Wedneseday.

Louisiana state climatologist Jay Grymes said he expected some pockets of flooding, but added, "With luck, this will be an in-and-out kind of situation."

Robbie Berg, a warning coordination meteorologist at the hurricane center, told The Associated Press that the storm's landfall itself shouldn't be too much of a concern.

"Landfall really doesn't have a whole lot of meaning in this particular case," Berg said.

Candice Henderson, who manages a beachside restaurant called the Crab Trap in Pensacola, told the AP that, for local residents, "this is just another storm." But officials in Florida, Louisiana and Mississippi still opened sites where people could acquire sandbags, while some beaches were closed to swimmers.

Warnings and watches in effect

Tropical storm watches were expanded Wednesday to include coastal parts of southwestern Louisiana and northeastern Texas as the storm traveled in their direction. Tropical storm warnings were in effect from the Alabama-Florida state line to Morgan City, Louisiana, as well as the area of New Orleans and Lake Pontchartrain.

A tropical storm watch was also posted for the area west of Morgan City to Sargent, Texas, and for Lake Maurepas in Louisiana.

"Tropical storm conditions will continue spreading across portions of the northern Gulf Coast within the warning area today," the hurricane center said early Wednesday. "Tropical storm conditions are possible within the watch area in Louisiana by tonight and along the upper Texas coast by Thursday or Thursday night."

The storm was expected to produce 1 to 4 inches of rain, with isolated totals of 6 inches tin some areas through Thursday. "This rainfall may produce isolated flash flooding, especially in urban areas," the hurricane center warned.

The system could also produce storm surge, raising waters up to 3 feet in some locations along the coast.

Bertha comes weeks after the 2026 hurricane season's first named storm, Tropical Storm Arthur, which made landfall in June along the Gulf Coast of Texas.

World.title: What Trump's generic drug tariffs could mean, according to experts
World.content:
Imported generic drugs could face tariffs of up to 100% beginning in 2028 under a plan announced Tuesday by President Trump, who said the measure is intended to push manufacturers to move production to the U.S.

Health policy experts said they are skeptical the tariffs alone would persuade generic drug manufacturers to relocate production to the U.S.

"A tariff can be part of a broader strategy, but is not going to by itself lead to onshoring," Marta Wosińska, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution's Center on Health Policy, said on Wednesday.

Mr. Trump announced Tuesday the 100% tariffs on generic drugmakers will begin in August 2028 and increase to 200% after one year.

"This is done in order to RESHORE Generic Pharmaceutical Production into America," the president wrote on Truth Social.

The measure could portend major changes for the generic drug industry, which accounts for 90% of prescriptions filled in the U.S., according to the Food and Drug Administration. Generic medications are manufactured with the same active ingredients as brand-name drugs but typically cost much less.

Generic drug manufacturing has increasingly shifted overseas during the past decades, with India now supplying more than 50% of the generic prescriptions filled in the U.S., according to a 2025 report by the Senate Committee on Aging.

The U.S. also relies heavily on China, which provides 95% and 70%, respectively, of imported ibuprofen and acetaminophen and as much as 45% of penicillin imports, the Coalition for a Prosperous America, a Washington, D.C.-based lobbying organization, said in a 2023 report.

Mr. Trump's plan provides a two-year runway for drug manufacturers to reshore production, White House spokesman Kush Desai told CBS News, who pointed to other administration policies such as full equipment expensing as aiding in the transition.

"The President's resounding success securing firm reshoring plans from global drugmakers as part of our most-favored-nations deals and Section 232 tariff program for branded drugs is proof that this administration has a track record of success to get critical manufacturing back into the United States," he said in an email.

Here's what experts say about the tariff's potential impact.

What would the tariffs mean for drug prices?

Generic drug manufacturers have slim margins, which could limit their ability to absorb the impact of tariffs, said Mariana Socal, an associate professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

"Any changes to the tariff structure are likely to be passed through to the consumer," she told CBS News.

Still, she added, competition and existing contracts may limit manufacturers' ability to immediately pass tariff costs on to buyers.

If consumers did see higher prices, the increases would be relatively modest because generic drugs are generally inexpensive, Wosińska said.

Would companies move their manufacturing operations?

The two-year timeline for reshoring generic drug production may be difficult to meet, experts said.

"These are facilities that require very specific equipment and infrastructure and quality standards," Socal said.

Companies will also need to consider whether the threat of tariffs is enough of an incentive to build manufacturing facilities in the U.S., where production expenses are higher, experts said.

"It is a large expense and manufacturers will weigh the potential upside of making the kind of initial investment versus what kind of profits they are going to make," Wosińska said.

The question is whether "a 200% tariff is going to be enough to justify that large of an upfront cost?" she added.

Teva Pharmaceuticals, an Israel-based company that's one of the world's largest generic drug producers, declined to comment on whether the company plans to expand manufacturing operations in the U.S. The company said its focus "remains on ensuring patients have access to high-quality, affordable medicines."

Sandoz, another leading generic drug producer headquartered in Switzerland, said generic medications are necessary for affordable healthcare in the U.S.

"We appreciate the administration's objective of strengthening domestic production and supply chain resilience for medicines in the United States," Sandoz CEO Richard Saynor said in a statement to CBS News.

He added, "To achieve that goal, policymakers and industry must work together to create a sustainable framework that enables long-term investment in generic and biosimilar medicines."

Experts said uncertainty surrounding U.S. tariff policy could also weigh on manufacturers' decisions. Trade policy has shifted dramatically over the last year, with the Supreme Court ruling in February that Mr. Trump lacked the authority to impose certain tariffs, invalidating a large portion of the levies he had imposed.

Would this impact drug availability?

The pressure from tariffs could prompt some manufacturers to exit the U.S. market altogether, resulting in supply shortages, Wosińska said.

She said she's concerned that "there is not going to be enough of an incentive for them to onshore. There is not going to be enough capacity if the tariffs were to come in, and manufacturers are just going to walk out of the market."

Those pharmaceutical companies could end up prioritizing other markets that already pay more for the drugs, Socal said. She cited research she conducted showing that manufacturing facilities that produce generic drugs for the U.S. market are, on average, also producing and selling to two additional global markets.

"Some large manufacturers may have the intended response from this policy, but some other manufacturers may simply choose not to sell, and that would be a big problem for us," she said.
