World.title: Her son was killed by ICE at a traffic stop. She says she's still waiting for justice
World.content:
Her son was killed by ICE at a traffic stop. She says she's still waiting for justice

toggle caption Brenda Bazán for NPR

When Rachel Reyes learned about the recent deaths of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero at the hands of federal immigration agents, she had flashbacks to what happened to her son 16 months ago.

"It really breaks my heart for the families because I understand the nightmare they're going through," Reyes says.

Her son, Ruben Ray Martinez, was fatally shot in March 2025 by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent during a traffic stop — like in the cases of Salgado Araujo and Durán Guerrero.

Sponsor Message

Martinez was killed two months into President Trump's return to office and the start of his aggressive immigration crackdown. Since then, there have been 29 additional instances in which immigration agents shot at civilians — at least seven of which turned deadly, according to The Trace, a nonprofit journalism site focused on gun violence. The Associated Press reports at least 10 fatalities during Trump's second term.

NPR reported on Martinez's death back in April — tracing his family's nearly yearlong saga to obtain body camera footage and for the case to be presented to a state grand jury, which later declined to bring charges against the agent who opened fire. Reyes says it's been difficult to watch history repeat itself, especially since she's still seeking accountability.

"It's just really upsetting, the whole thing, because I know what it feels like, and it's incredibly frustrating to be treated like if your loved one's life doesn't matter," she says. Reyes, who is from San Antonio, Texas, recently wrote about the need for greater transparency and accountability in ICE shootings in an op-ed for The New York Times.

toggle caption Brenda Bazán for NPR

Deadly encounters, once again at traffic stops

Martinez, a 23-year-old U.S. citizen, was fatally shot in the early hours of March 15, 2025, on South Padre Island, a resort destination in south Texas. After a night spent celebrating his birthday, Martinez approached a busy intersection, where a car crash had taken place hours earlier. Officers from multiple agencies were on scene to help manage traffic, including Homeland Security Investigations, which is part of ICE.

Sponsor Message

When reached for comment, the Department of Homeland Security told NPR the driver "intentionally ran over" an HSI officer, which sent him onto the hood of Martinez's blue Ford. "Upon witnessing this, another agent fired defensive shots to protect himself, his fellow agents, and the general public," DHS added. The agency said the officer who made contact with the car "sustained a knee injury and was taken to the hospital."

But footage from state and local officers' body cameras, released by the Texas Department of Public Safety, shows Martinez was given conflicting directions before he slowly drove forward and to the left. It's also unclear from the videos reviewed by NPR whether the vehicle struck an agent.

DHS gave similar accounts in the cases of Salgado Araujo in Texas and Durán Guerrero in Maine, who were killed in the span of a week this month. In both cases, the agency said the two men attempted to flee traffic stops and weaponized their vehicles. In Maine, DHS said the ICE officer feared "for public safety" before firing his weapon. But the federal government has yet to release video evidence that supports those claims. Two passengers in the van driven by Salgado Araujo have disputed ICE's accounts, Houston Public Media reported. In both incidents, ICE agents were not wearing body cameras.

Beyond shooting incidents, a recent American Civil Liberties Union report found dozens of incidents across eight states since January 2025 where immigration officers rammed into people's cars, smashed vehicle windows and struck people with cars.

Last week, following the two deadly traffic stops, NPR reported that DHS planned to halt nonurgent vehicle stops. But a day after the reports of a policy shift, Trump posted on Truth Social that they must continue.

"We CANNOT give up one of I.C.E.'s most important and effective Crime Fighting tools, THE TRAFFIC STOP!" he wrote. "Once we do, we are playing right into the criminal's hands."

Sponsor Message

At a press briefing on Thursday, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt further added that vehicle stops are "a necessary tool that ICE agents need in order to continue their deportation campaign."

A long, difficult legal process

In Martinez's case, it took 11 months for DHS to publicly acknowledge its involvement. It only came to light after American Oversight, a watchdog group, filed a public records request for documents related to ICE's use of force. In late February, a grand jury in Texas declined to bring criminal charges against the federal agent who killed Martinez. Rachel Reyes' attorney Charles Stam says they're currently exploring all legal options.

"If a U.S. citizen killed by an ICE agent cannot get a serious federal investigation or an admission of fault, imagine the odds facing families whose immigration status is precarious, who lack legal representation, or whose loved one's death did not happen to be caught on camera," Stam says.

Meanwhile, in Minnesota, it remains unclear if the federal immigration agents responsible for the deaths of U.S. citizens Renee Macklin Good and Alex Pretti back in January will be charged. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said last Monday her office finally received evidence that was previously withheld by the Justice Department, including hard drives containing statements and body camera footage, according to MPR News.

Meanwhile, Minnesota has charged an ICE agent in a nonfatal shooting of a Venezuelan man, also in January. But prosecuting federal agents can be difficult and is relatively rare since they typically have broad legal protections while carrying out their duties.

Reyes says she hoped for change and a decrease in deadly encounters with ICE when Markwayne Mullin took over leadership of the Department of Homeland Security in March. But after the recent shootings, Reyes feels at a loss about what it will take to see accountability and justice for families who lose a loved one to an immigration agent.

Sponsor Message

" It shouldn't be our new normal," she says. "They're destroying more families with all this chaos, and it's not right."

World.title: How does the new Gordie Howe bridge deal compare to the original one?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

You wouldn't be blamed for feeling a little lost when it comes to recent news about the Gordie Howe International Bridge.

Earlier this month, Canada and the U.S. announced a fresh pact to open the long-awaited span connecting Ontario and Michigan after months of uncertainty over its future.

But the terms of that deal were opaque, at best, with top officials from each country offering differing interpretations — specifically around revenue sharing and how Canada's debt to build the $6.4-billion border crossing plays into that.

After much criticism and speculation, Canada posted the text of the agreement online late Tuesday night.

But there's also a deal from 2012 that includes some toll revenue splitting. The text of the new pact says it doesn't change anything in the 2012 agreement.

So what's the difference?

The key to understanding it is that the 2012 deal is for sharing toll revenue with the state of Michigan many years down the road, while the most recent agreement is for sharing revenue with an economic development fund controlled by the U.S. federal government for the first 15 years.

Let's break down what we know about how that will work, ahead of the official opening of the bridge in the coming days.

The 2012 Canada-Michigan crossing agreement

In June 2012, then Prime Minister Stephen Harper and Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder announced their respective governments had struck a deal to build a still-unnamed bridge connecting Windsor and Detroit.

When they were in office in 2012, Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder and Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper, left to right, announced a deal had been struck to build a new bridge connecting Windsor and Detroit. (Colin Perkins/The Canadian Press)

The over 50-page agreement laid out the legal and financial structures underpinning the project, which had an estimated cost of $1 billion at the time.

The deal was a major step forward to build a new span within the busiest land border crossing in North America, especially given the issue of commercial truck traffic clogging city streets leading to the nearly century-old Ambassador Bridge.

Canada's willingness to pay for the new project came as Michigan was still reeling from the 2008 financial crisis.

"That’s what friendship is all about — stepping up and helping someone," Snyder said at the announcement. "A special note of thanks to Canada, for your generosity and thoughtfulness in this project."

Under the agreement, Canada would fund construction of the bridge, Canadian inspection plaza, land acquisitions and a new interchange with the I-75 highway on the Michigan side.

As a result, tolls would be collected only on the Canadian side, with the revenue used to pay down the cost of the project — something the agreement said could take at least 50 years.

Once the debt is paid off, Canada will split the toll revenue with Michigan, which co-owns the bridge, per the deal.

It also said the crossing authority — now known as the Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority — "shall be entitled to set rates" for tolls.

The 2026 Canada-U.S. 'agreement in principle'

Much has changed since then, especially in Washington. U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war has eroded the Canada-U.S. relationship, and he made the bridge the target of his ire earlier this year, with a social media outburst laced with falsehoods about the project and demanding that Canada provide concessions.

That post, which followed heavy lobbying and political donations from the owners of the Ambassador Bridge, sparked concerns about when the Gordie Howe crossing would actually open to the public.

The Gordie Howe bridge from the Canadian side in June. Canada posted the text of the new bridge agreement online late Tuesday. (Jacob Barker/CBC)

After a false start last month, both governments announced on July 10 that they had reached a fresh pact to open the bridge.

Under that agreement, toll revenue will be used to pay operating expenses, such as maintenance, snow removal and staffing. Whatever is left over — if anything — will get split in half. Canada will get one half, and the rest will go to an economic development fund "established and solely controlled" by the U.S. government.

That setup will last for 15 years. Canada will be able to use its half to start paying down the debt, while the other half will be used "for the benefit of the United States and trade between Canada and the United States," according to the deal.

In other words, Canada will still start paying down its debt immediately with whatever net revenues it gets, but those revenues will be smaller than before. And whenever the debt is paid off, the revenue will get still get split with Michigan.

The new deal also gives the U.S. government control over some changes to toll rates — something it didn't have before.

Canadian officials will host a ribbon-cutting event on Friday before the bridge opens to traffic on Monday.

World.title: Ontario's emergency preparedness minister defends wildfire response as staff cuts radio interview short
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ontario Emergency Preparedness Minister Jill Dunlop defended the province's wildfire response on CBC Radio on Tuesday, but her staff abruptly cut the interview short after she was asked to respond to criticism from community leaders.

With wildfires burning across much of northwestern Ontario , Dunlop's office is responsible for co-ordinating emergency evacuations, shelter and wraparound services for people fleeing the flames.

Several community leaders, including First Nations chiefs , have criticized the province's emergency response as slow, disorganized and unco-ordinated.

When As It Happens host Nil Köksal raised those concerns with Dunlop, the minister said her department has had "co-ordination calls every day with the communities to ensure that we're working hand-in-hand and that they have the most up-to-date information."

But immediately after Dunlop answered the question, one of the minister's staff members interrupted the call, saying it was time to "wrap it up."

LISTEN | Interview with Emergency Preparedness Minister Jill Dunlop: As It Happens 7:26 Ontario's emergency preparedness minister defends wildfire response in interview cut short Ontario Emergency Preparedness Minister Jill Dunlop defended the province's wildfire response during an interview with As It Happens host Nil Köksal, but her staff abruptly cut the interview short after she was asked to respond to criticism from community leaders.

"We still have a few more questions," Köksal said, asking for three more minutes to complete the interview.

"Um, no," the staffer said.

"Why would the minister not want to answer the questions of her constituents?" Köksal asked.

"She has," the staffer said, before hanging up.

CBC News reached out to the minister's office to ask why the interview ended early and to give Dunlop an opportunity to respond to unanswered questions, but did not receive a response before deadline.

'Too many delays and too many gaps'

As of Wednesday, there were 146 active wildfires burning in Ontario, and 2,415 people had been evacuated from 13 communities.

The communities of Namaygoosisagagun First Nation and Whitewater Lake First Nation have been completely destroyed. First Nations chiefs in Ontario have called for a public inquiry into the wildfire response .

Chief Alvin Fiddler is grand chief of Nishnawbe Aski Nation, which represents Whitewater Lake. He spoke to As It Happens on Monday about how the fires have impacted his people.

"There's been too many delays and too many gaps in the response," Fiddler said, singling out Dunlop specifically.

Grand Chief Alvin Fiddler of Nishnawbe Aski Nation reacts as Chief Pauline Drake of Whitewater First Nation recounts her community's evacuation. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press)

Lawrence Wanakamik, chief of the recently evacuated Whitesand First Nation, told the program last week that community members have not been getting timely information from the province about the status of the fires or efforts to fight them.

"They are getting anxious, worried and some of them are getting a little bit angry," he said.

When asked how she responded to frustrations expressed by Fiddler and other community leaders, Dunlop said she has been in communication with Fiddler since he first spoke to As It Happens.

She also noted there are two provincial departments responding to the fires, and she can only answer for her own.

"There's the Ministry of Natural Resources, who is dealing directly with fires, there's the Ministry of Emergency Preparedness and Response, and we're dealing with the evacuations," she said.

Emily McLaughlin, a spokesperson for Natural Resources Minister Mike Harris, says the department "meets year-round with Indigenous communities on wildfire preparedness planning."

"We are in constant contact with First Nations communities and have taken action to improve co-ordination this fire season, including requesting assistance from the federal government, to speed up evacuations and supports," she said in an emailed statement.

"We will continue to support evacuations of communities impacted by the wildland fires while deploying all available supports and resources needed, as quickly as possible."

'We were not prepared'

On Friday, the province announced it will spend $650 million on five new helicopters and six new water bombers .

But Wanakamik said that is "a little too late for that."

"The climate change has been getting worse over the years," he said. "The governments should have actually been on those things."

This year’s budget shows the province spent $271 million on emergency firefighting in 2025-26, but plans to spend $150 million in 2026-27.

However, the province has said it will access a contingency fund to cover any costs beyond what is budgeted.

"Our government will not spare a single penny to protect Ontario communities and keep people safe," McLaughlin said.

WATCH | Opposition calls out Ford government over wildfire response: Is the Ford government doing enough to fight wildfires? Opposition says no. | Duration 2:37 Premier Doug Ford has pledged that the province will spend whatever is necessary to combat the fires, but opposition parties argue Ontario was not adequately prepared for this year's wildfire season. CBC's Shawn Jeffords breaks down what we know.

Sharon Bak, a former field officer with Emergency Management Ontario, said the province has had decades to get its ducks in a row but has failed to do so.

She now works as a volunteer community emergency management co-ordinator for the unincorporated municipality of Pass Lake.

In an interview with As It Happens last week, she raised concerns about a lack of emergency planning for unincorporated communities, noting that work has largely been done by volunteers with no funding.

"I'm doing it off the side of my desk as a freebie to my community because I love my community. I grew up there. I want it to be safe," she said. "I'm angry. I'm upset."

Harris' office did not specifically respond to questions from CBC News about emergency response in unincorporated communities.

At a press conference on Thursday, Harris said: "We really encourage all communities, especially in the North, to have emergency management plans and work with us."

Fiddler said First Nations have been trying to do just that.

"We had a similar severe fire emergency situation back in 2021, and we had created a plan and a proposal for First Nations to have more ownership of emergency management in our territory," he said.

"I hand-delivered that package to Premier Doug Ford. He took my proposal, but there's been zero response. And that was five years ago."

World.title: Manitoba 'willing to entertain' Alberta to Ontario pipeline: Kinew
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew says he's open to a west-east pipeline being pitched by his counterparts in Alberta and Ontario.

Kinew says the pipeline could make Canada stronger and there are workers in his province who would be eager to help build it.

But he says major projects such as pipelines need to be built the right way, by addressing environmental concerns and bringing Indigenous governments on board.

Speaking at a meeting of premiers in Charlottetown, Kinew says he's "willing to entertain" the pipeline proposal announced by Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Ontario Premier Doug Ford earlier this month.

The line would stretch 3,300 kilometres from Hardisty, Alta., to refineries in Sarnia, Ont., going through Saskatchewan and Manitoba and not crossing into the U.S.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe previously said he's on board.

Smith and Ford have said the pipeline would move 500,000 barrels of crude per day and reduce Canada's need to import refined oil.

Ontario is expected to finish a feasibility study, with a price tag and a building schedule, before the end of the year.

World.title: Trump's trade rep defends new tariffs on Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump's point man on trade is justifying the plan to slap new tariffs of 50 per cent on many Canadian products as part of a broader strategy aimed at reducing the U.S. trade deficit.

The trade deficit, which hit $1.2 trillion US in 2025, is a "national emergency," U.S. trade representative Jamieson Greer told a Senate finance committee hearing on Wednesday.

"That national emergency still persists, and so our policy remains the same," Greer said. "We are committed to continuing to use tariffs and to negotiate deals to support the re-industrialization of our economy, protect American workers and increase their wages and shrink our trade deficit."

Following the hearing, CBC News asked Greer to explain the timing of Trump's move to put new tariffs on Canadian products ranging from plywood to milk.

"This is something that's been in preparation for some time," Greer told CBC's Katie Nicholson.

He said the tariffs are "very tailored" to respond to Canadian trade actions that affect the U.S. alcohol, dairy and auto sectors.

WATCH | What Greer told U.S. senators: Greer hopes to have 'options' ready on trade with Canada, Mexico this year | Duration 2:01 U.S. trade representative Jamieson Greer says he hopes to have 'options' for President Donald Trump and the 'leaders of Canada and or Mexico to consider' by the end of the year around the critical trade deal known as CUSMA in Canada and USMCA in the U.S.

"We have tried for over a year to get the Canadians to eliminate these things."

"We've given them the best treatment available in the world in the past year or so, and despite that, they've still taken these actions, so we thought it was necessary to elevate this."

During the committee hearing, several Democrat senators gave Greer heat over the tariffs, which are due to take effect on Aug. 19 and apply to some $20 billion US worth of Canada's annual exports.

Greer wants 'options'

Greer also faced questions on the status of the broader renegotiation of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA).

He said he is hopeful of having "options" for some form of deals with both Canada and Mexico in 2026.

"I would love to have, between now and and the end of the year, at least some arrangements, one with Canada, one with Mexico," Greer said.

"I'm hopeful that before the end of the year, we can have at least options for President Trump and the leaders of Canada and/or Mexico to consider."

Sen. Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the committee, accused the administration of having "lost the plot" on tariffs.

"Just a few days ago, Canada, our closest neighbour, basically learned they were going to get 50 per cent tariffs. At the same time, when it comes to China, one of the biggest trade cheats there is, it seems that the administration rolls out the red carpet," Wyden told the hearing.

Some Canadian goods face higher tariffs than China

Greer pushed back on Wyden's claim that the Trump administration is giving China more favourable trade terms than Canada. He said only "a small handful" of Canadian products will face higher tariffs than those that originate in China.

He also disputed other Democratic senators' concerns that the latest tariff move against Canada will hurt U.S. farmers and exporters' access to Canadian markets or face Canadian retaliation.

"I talked with my Canadian counterpart yesterday. They did not say they're going to retaliate," Greer said. Although he did not name his "Canadian counterpart," Greer's equivalent in Ottawa is Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc.

World.title: 911 outage affecting all of Manitoba outside of Winnipeg
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The emergency 911 service is currently down for all Manitoba communities except for Winnipeg, after the service went down at the dispatch centre in Brandon on Wednesday.

Residents in Brandon who need help should call the police non-emergency line at 204-729-2345 for an officer, as efforts are underway to restore service, Brandon police said in a warning on social media Wednesday afternoon .

Residents in other municipalities are encouraged to use their local 10-digit emergency phone numbers until the issue is resolved, the Brandon police social media post said.

The province sent out an alert via cellphones about the outage around 2:45 p.m. on Wednesday.

An alert sent to cellphones in Manitoba on Wednesday warning of a 911 outage for communities outside Winnipeg. (CBC)

There are two primary 911 emergency dispatch centres in Manitoba: one in Brandon and one in Winnipeg.

The Brandon emergency dispatch centre also provides 911 service to communities across Manitoba outside of Winnipeg, serving seven police agencies and nearly 200 fire departments, including Brandon itself and many rural areas across Manitoba.

Winnipeg police said in a post on X the 911 service is working normally in the city.

Brandon Police Service communications specialist Janet Reichert said the police force is working with the City of Brandon and Bell MTS to get the service back up.

In a statement, the telecom company said it is investigating a suspected third-party fibre cut and is "working to restore service as quickly as possible."

Both Brandon police and Bell said they will provide updates on the 911 service as they're available.

World.title: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt’s daughter Vivienne files to drop Pitt's last name
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie's daughter Vivienne wants to legally remove "Pitt" from her last name. She's the latest of their six kids to legally file to drop their father's surname.

According to documents obtained by CBC News, she filed a petition with the Los Angeles County Superior Court to change her legal name from Vivienne Marcheline Jolie-Pitt to Vivienne Marcheline Jolie.

She signed the request on July 12 — her 18th birthday — and filed it Monday. The reason for the change is listed as "personal." Under California law, turning 18 allows her to do this on her own without parent or guardian approval.

This isn't a total surprise to fans keeping up with the family. Back in 2024, she was credited as Vivienne Jolie for her work on the Broadway show The Outsiders, which Angelina produced. And she's not the first to make the change.

Angelina Jolie and her children (left to right) Maddox, Vivienne, Zahara, Shiloh and Knox arrive for the world premiere of Marvel Studios' Eternals at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles in 2021. (Valerie Macon/AFP/Getty Images)

Pitt and Jolie have six children together: Maddox, 24; Pax, 22; Zahara, 21; Shiloh, 20; Knox, 18 and Vivienne.

Shiloh dropped Pitt from her name in 2024. And earlier this year, both Zahara and Maddox filed paperwork to do the same. In the credits for Jolie's film Couture — which Maddox worked on as an assistant director — he was credited as Maddox Jolie.

The news comes after years of reported tension within the family following the A-list couple's 2016 split, stemming from court-documented allegations detailed during Pitt and Jolie's lengthy legal battle.

In that time, Jolie alleged Pitt grabbed her by the head and shook her, choked one of their children and struck another when they tried to defend her. A representative for Pitt denied the allegations. An FBI statement said it conducted a review of the circumstances and did not pursue further investigation.

After over a decade together and two years of marriage, their protracted divorce was officially finalized in 2024.

Pitt has been public about his issues with alcohol and efforts to quit drinking, which he says began in 2016. He has credited Alcoholics Anonymous with helping him stay sober for nearly a decade.

He has not been seen in public or photographed with any of his kids for years, unlike Jolie who is often seen with them on carpets and speaks about them in interviews.

CBC News reached out to Pitt's representation for comment but hasn't received a response.

A hearing for Vivienne's request is set for Nov. 2, and was originally set for Oct. 30.

World.title: New wildfire near Boston Bar, B.C., quadruples in size overnight
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A new wildfire discovered near Boston Bar, B.C., on Tuesday more than quadrupled in size overnight.

Logged at 10 square kilometres (1,000 hectares) Tuesday night, the B.C. Wildfire Service (BCWS) estimated the fire had grown to 43.3 sq. km (4,332 ha) as of Wednesday morning.

The wildfire service said the Anderson Creek fire started beside Highway 1, just south of Boston Bar, and "spread rapidly upslope."

"Aggressive fire behaviour (fast-moving crown fire) continued into the night," BCWS said in a response update.

The Anderson Creek fire joins a wildfire complex already burning in the area, on either side of the Fraser River. The Brunswick Creek and Ainslie Creek wildfires together spanned an area that grew to about 234 square kilometres (23,438.3 hectares) as of Wednesday, according to BCWS.

All three are considered "wildfires of note."

Morgan Blois, BCWS information officer, said the upslope movement of the Anderson Creek wildfire has created a lot of energy, which increased the fire behaviour on the Brunswick Creek wildfire.

The service said crews anticipate "another challenging day" Wednesday due to hot and very dry conditions.

Blois said the service is expecting "fairly extreme vigorous fire behaviour."

The size of the wildfires burning near Boston Bar, B.C., as of Tuesday, July 21. The fire V11090 has since been named Anderson Creek. (CBC News)

BCWS said fire behaviour and steep terrain on the Brunswick Creek wildfire made direct attack unsafe for ground crews on Tuesday. Tactics are being "reassessed" while structure crews engage in structure defence.

"Even light winds will increase fire activity and change fire behaviour rapidly, particularly in unburnt areas within the perimeter and where challenging terrain has limited suppression options," said the BCWS.

All three fires are suspected to be human-caused, which is how any wildfire not sparked by lightning is categorized.

The Fraser Valley Regional District (FVRD), which had previously issued an evacuation order for Boston Bar, sent an urgent alert Tuesday ordering any residents remaining in the community to leave immediately.

District board chair Patricia Ross said the fire is "pretty frightening."

"There are still people that are refusing to leave. They absolutely must leave," she said.

"This moves so fast, it's nothing to fool around with."

She said it has been too unsafe to get more updates regarding structure loss, and noted the firefight has been very difficult.

Prior to the Anderson Creek wildfire, Ross said there were about 450 properties in the regional district affected by the evacuation orders and alerts but she noted that not all the properties had homes on them.

Highway 1 is closed in both directions between Anderson River Mainline and Jackass Summit for 41.2 kilometres due to the wildfires, according to DriveBC.

Highway 5 should be used as an alternate route, DriveBC said.

Wildfires of note near Kimberley

Two more wildfires are considered "of note" by the BCWS near Kimberley in southeast B.C.

The Tower Creek 2 wildfire was burning at 2.5 sq. km. (250 hectares) and the Matthew Creek was burning an area of 5.67 sq. km. (567 hectares) earlier Wednesday.

The wildfire service said fire activity was subdued overnight on both wildfires but it expects fire activity to pick up in the afternoon on Wednesday during the warmest and driest part of the day.

The City of Kimberley and Regional District of East Kootenay have issued evacuation alerts due to the wildfires.

There are about 89 wildfires burning across B.C. as of Wednesday afternoon.

World.title: Coalition calls on culture minister to withdraw criticism of human rights museum's Nakba exhibit
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A coalition of civil society groups is pushing back against criticism by a federal cabinet minister and Jewish organizations of an exhibit on Palestinian displacement at a national museum in Winnipeg.

The Canadian Museum for Human Rights, a federal Crown corporation in Winnipeg, has faced a torrent of criticism over its exhibit on the Nakba — Arabic for "catastrophe." It's the term Palestinians use to describe Israel's declaration of independence in 1948, which led to the displacement of hundreds of thousands of people.

Culture Minister Marc Miller has said the museum failed by not naming Hamas in the exhibit, which opened to the public on June 27, as a terrorist organization that targets Jews, while Jewish and civil society groups say the exhibit portrays only one side of a complex history.

Dozens of groups issued a joint statement Wednesday voicing support for the museum and pushing back against what they call political interference in its operations.

Curator Isabelle Masson views the exhibit, Palestine Uprooted —Nakba Past and Present, that she created at the Canadian Museum for Human Rights on June 26. (John Woods/The Canadian Press)

"As publicly funded institutions governed by the public interest, museums dedicated to human rights have a responsibility to confront difficult, contested, and often painful histories. This exhibition reflects that responsibility," the letter says.

"We are particularly concerned that calls for political intervention have, in some instances, extended beyond public advocacy into commentary from elected officials regarding the content of the exhibition."

The letter's 74 signatories include Amnesty International, the United Church of Canada, Independent Jewish Voices and the Union of National Employees, which represents most of the Winnipeg museum staff.

They wrote political leaders should respect the independence of museums and "refrain from influencing or appearing to influence curatorial decisions" in the face of what they call an organized pressure campaign.

The Canadian Press has contacted Miller's office for comment.
