Both partners frame the decision as a cost play. Doubling output lowers the unit cost of each tonne produced, which improves margins even if prices stay flat.

The move also positions Covalent to capture cash flow quickly when a sustained recovery in electric vehicle demand tightens the global lithium market.

How SQM Fits into the Global Picture

SQM’s lithium business spans Chile, Australia, and China, supplying giants like LG Energy Solution and Tesla. The company has been racing to expand capacity while rivals pull back, a contrarian bet that it can serve a market expected to triple in size by 2035.

The Mt Holland expansion reinforces that strategy. By securing more hard-rock supply, SQM complements its brine operations and builds a portfolio that can respond flexibly to shifts in battery chemistry and customer demand.

For foreign investors watching Latin America’s commodity champions, the message is clear: SQM is no longer just a Chilean story.

What This Means for Expats and Investors

For expatriates and foreign investors with ties to Latin America, SQM’s Australian expansion signals a maturation of the region’s commodity giants into truly global players. The company is using cash generated from its Chilean brine operations to fund growth in a stable, mining-friendly jurisdiction, which could reduce the risk profile of its overall business.

Investors who track SQM on the New York Stock Exchange should note that the Mt Holland project adds a hard-rock pillar to a portfolio long dominated by brine extraction. This diversification may offer a buffer against regulatory changes in Chile, where lithium nationalization debates have periodically rattled markets.

The expansion also ties SQM more closely to Asian battery supply chains that depend on Australian spodumene.

What Happens Next

Construction on the second concentrator and ore-sorting facility is expected to ramp up over the next several years, with first production targeted for 2030. In the near term, the partners will focus on detailed engineering and procurement contracts, while continuing to operate the existing concentrator at full capacity.

The global lithium market will be watching closely. If electric vehicle sales accelerate in the second half of the decade as many analysts forecast, Covalent Lithium could be bringing new supply online just as demand outstrips current production capacity.

For now, SQM and Wesfarmers are placing a long-term wager that the energy transition remains on track.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Covalent Lithium joint venture?

Covalent Lithium is a 50/50 partnership between Chilean miner SQM and Australia’s Wesfarmers, a diversified industrial conglomerate with retail, chemical, and mining interests. The venture operates the Mt Holland mine and processing assets in Western Australia, producing spodumene concentrate for the global battery supply chain.

Why are SQM and Wesfarmers expanding during low lithium prices?

The expansion is designed to lower unit operating costs by spreading fixed expenses over a larger production base. This improves profitability even if prices remain subdued, and it positions the venture to capture significant cash flow quickly when electric vehicle demand pushes lithium prices higher.

How much lithium will the expanded Mt Holland project produce?

Once the second concentrator is online around 2030, the mine will produce 760,000 tonnes of spodumene concentrate per year, double its current capacity of 380,000 tonnes. The new ore-sorting facility will also recover an additional 3 million tonnes of material over the life of the mine from stockpiles previously considered waste.

World.title: Argentina Leads Latin American Charge at Cincinnati Open
World.content:
Latin American tennis will field one of its deepest contingents of the season at the 2026 Cincinnati Open, with 14 players from six countries currently listed across the ATP and WTA singles fields. The group includes 12 men and two women, led by Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo, Brazil’s João Fonseca, Peru’s Ignacio Buse, Chile’s Alejandro Tabilo, and — in the women’s draw — Colombia’s Camila Osorio and Brazil’s Beatriz Haddad Maia.

Argentina accounts for eight of the entrants, giving the country by far the largest Latin American delegation at the combined ATP and WTA 1000 tournament. The published lists remain subject to withdrawals and other changes before the draws are completed. Rankings attached to the entries are entry-list positions, not finalized tournament seeds.

Cerúndolo arrives as Latin America’s highest-ranked entrant, listed at No. 22 after producing one of the strongest seasons of his career. The 27-year-old won the Buenos Aires title in February before capturing his first ATP 500 trophy at Queen’s Club in June. That victory made him the first Argentine man to win the historic grass-court tournament and moved him back toward the world’s top 20.

Fonseca will be another major attraction. The 19-year-old Brazilian is listed at No. 28 after reaching his first ATP Masters 1000 quarterfinal in Monte Carlo and making a breakthrough run to the Roland Garros quarterfinals.

Fonseca’s Paris run included a third-round, five-set comeback from two sets down against Novak Djokovic — a result that made him the first teenager in three decades to win back-to-back Grand Slam matches from two sets down, and the first to oust a former Roland Garros champion from that deficit since Michael Chang. He followed it by beating Casper Ruud to reach the last eight before falling to Jakub Mensik in the quarterfinals.

Cerúndolo and Fonseca are joined inside the tournament’s published top 32 by Tabilo at No. 30 and Argentina’s Tomás Martín Etcheverry at No. 31. Those four players would be positioned to receive seeds if the rankings and field remain similar when the draw is made. Final seedings, however, will be determined closer to the tournament and could shift because of ranking changes or withdrawals.

Etcheverry won his first ATP Tour title at the Rio Open in February, defeating Tabilo in the final after completing two matches on the tournament’s final day. The result gave Argentina another established contender beyond Cerúndolo. Tabilo has also been showing improved form. In addition to reaching the Rio final, the Chilean advanced to the semifinals in Båstad in July before losing a close three-set match to Andrey Rublev.

Buse may be the most important player sitting just outside the projected seed line. The 22-year-old Peruvian is listed at No. 35 following a remarkable rise that included winning the ATP 500 tournament in Hamburg as a qualifier. His victory over Tommy Paul in the Hamburg final made Buse the first Peruvian to win an ATP singles title since Luis Horna in 2007. He later became the first Peruvian man in more than three decades to win a Wimbledon main-draw singles match.

Argentina’s full group also includes Sebastián Báez at No. 56, Román Andrés Burruchaga at No. 60, Juan Manuel Cerúndolo at No. 50, Mariano Navone at No. 47, Thiago Agustín Tirante at No. 57 and Camilo Ugo Carabelli at No. 69. Navone has already collected a significant result this season, winning his first ATP Tour title in Bucharest in April.

Paraguay will be represented by Adolfo Daniel Vallejo, listed at No. 63. Vallejo recently reached the Båstad semifinals, where he pushed defending champion Luciano Darderi to three sets and became the first Paraguayan to reach an ATP Tour semifinal since Ramón Delgado in 2002.

Two women from the region appear in the published WTA field. Osorio, Colombia’s long-time No. 1, is joined by Haddad Maia, a former world No. 10 and 2023 Roland Garros semifinalist who is the most decorated Latin American woman in the draw. The regional representation still tilts heavily toward the men’s tournament, where Argentina alone accounts for eight entrants.

The Cincinnati Open will begin with qualifying on August 11, followed by main-draw competition and the men’s and women’s singles finals on August 23.

The tournament features 96-player singles fields and is one of five events that stage ATP and WTA 1000 competitions at the same location. Its expanded format followed a $260 million redevelopment of the Lindner Family Tennis Center in Mason, Ohio. For Latin American players, Cincinnati represents both an opportunity to collect valuable ranking points and a final major test against elite competition before the US Open.

World.title: Archaeologists Exhume Nearly 3,000-Year-Old Remains Near San Salvador
World.content:
Archaeologists exhumed human remains estimated to be nearly 3,000 years old on the outskirts of San Salvador, the Ministry of Culture said in a statement. The remains form part of a pre-Hispanic burial discovered at the Pasaje 4 archaeological site in Antiguo Cuscatlán, a district in the metropolitan area of San Salvador (municipality of La Libertad Este). Officials estimate the remains date to around 850 B.C.

The burial also contained a small Usulután-style ceramic vessel shaped like a sea turtle. Excavators additionally uncovered two ancient cassava (yuca) cultivation furrows preserved beneath layers of volcanic ash from eruptions in different periods — one associated with the Plan de la Laguna eruption around 850 B.C. and another linked to the Ilopango Caldera eruption between approximately 431 and 539 A.D.

The human remains were found face down (in a prone position, oriented about 17 degrees east of north). They will undergo radiocarbon testing to confirm their exact age. DNA analysis will also be conducted to help determine the individual’s sex and other biological details. Archaeologist Carlos Flores Manzano, a doctoral candidate at Yale University who directed the excavation under the supervision of the National Directorate of Cultural Heritage, noted that the burial appears to have been prepared before the volcanic event rather than resulting from it.

According to the official report, the area may hold a similar number of remains to those found at Structure E3-7 at the Chalchuapa archaeological site in western El Salvador. There, salvage excavations in 1977–1978 recovered the remains of 33 individuals, widely interpreted as evidence of human sacrifice and among the earliest such documented cases in the Mesoamerican region.

That assemblage included 26 complete skeletons, four partial skeletons, and three isolated skulls. Many were found face down; some showed signs that hands or feet had been bound or were absent, along with evidence of mutilation and decapitation. The individuals whose sex could be determined were adult males, and researchers have suggested they may have been war captives.

The Antiguo Cuscatlán finds build on earlier archaeological work in the same zone, including a 1987 rescue excavation by Paul Amaroli and Gregorio Bello-Suazo. Further laboratory analysis of the newly recovered remains and associated materials is expected to refine the dating and provide additional insight into pre-Hispanic occupation and agricultural practices in the region prior to major volcanic events.

World.title: Costa Rica Plans Integrated Train and Bus Network to Ease Traffic Congestion
World.content:
Costa Rica’s national railway institute is pushing to link the country’s trains, buses, and taxis into a single coordinated network, a plan its backers say could finally give commuters in the capital region a faster alternative to sitting in traffic.

The Instituto Costarricense de Ferrocarriles (Incofer) is promoting what it calls an intermodal public transport system, designed so that different modes of travel connect smoothly rather than competing for the same passengers. The aim is to shorten travel times and improve mobility across the Greater Metropolitan Area, the densely populated ring of cities spanning San José, Alajuela, Heredia, and Cartago where most of the chronic congestion is concentrated. Incofer is developing the scheme alongside the Cámara Nacional de Transportes (Canatrans), the national transport chamber that represents the country’s bus operators.

The plan is built around the Tren Eléctrico de Pasajeros, the electric passenger train that Incofer intends to make the backbone of public transport in the region. Under the proposal, buses would operate as feeder routes, carrying passengers from their neighborhoods to nearby rail stations, where they could transfer and continue by train to destinations elsewhere in the metropolitan area.

Taxis and other services would handle the shorter first- and last-mile connections at either end of a journey. Incofer and Canatrans argue that coordinating routes this way would cut the wasteful duplication that has buses and trains running parallel to one another today, and make transfers quick enough that public transport becomes a real option for people who now drive.

Technology is central to the pitch. The project envisions tools that would let a passenger plan a full trip across several modes at once, potentially including unified payment and real-time information on routes, schedules, and fares, so that moving from a bus to a train feels like one continuous journey rather than a series of disconnected legs.

Canatrans has framed the effort as a way to reduce dependence on private vehicles, which it identifies as one of the main drivers of the region’s gridlock. With Costa Rica recently ranked among the worst countries in the world for traffic, authorities hope that drawing more commuters onto a coordinated public network would ease that pressure over time.

The intermodal plan rests on a project that has moved unusually fast this year after decades of false starts. In May the Legislative Assembly approved the international financing for the electric train, tracked under file number 25.291, and President Laura Fernández Delgado signed the financing law shortly afterward. Incofer executive president Álvaro Bermúdez Peña called the approval a historic step toward a modern, efficient transport system.

The financing package draws on international lenders that include the Central American Bank for Economic Integration, the European Union, and the Green Climate Fund. As designed, the system would run along roughly 52 kilometers (32 miles) of double electrified track connecting the four Greater Metropolitan Area provinces, add a fleet of new electric trains, and lift daily ridership from about 16,000 passengers today toward a target of 100,000.

As of now, the intermodal component remains a framework rather than a finished plan. Neither Incofer nor Canatrans has published implementation timelines, the investment required to reorganize bus routes, or the locations of the transfer points where the connections would happen. Both institutions maintain, however, that no amount of new rail infrastructure will relieve congestion on its own, and that the trains only deliver on their promise if the buses and taxis around them are organized to feed passengers in and out.

World.title: Salvadoran herbal tea eyes Belize market as promoters tout benefits for patients with kidney disease and renal failure
World.content:
Salvadoran herbal tea eyes Belize market as promoters tout benefits for patients with kidney disease and renal failure

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Chinese-inspired herbal tea manufactured in El Salvador could soon become available in Belize, with its developers promoting it as a natural supplement for people living with kidney disease and several other chronic health conditions.

The product is marketed under the name Té She Yin Cheng, also written as Té Sheyin Cheng, and was developed by natural-medicine practitioner She Yin Cheng, who has lived and operated businesses in El Salvador for several decades.

During an interview, Cheng said the product is based on principles of Chinese herbal medicine and has gained recognition among doctors and patients in El Salvador. He said his goal is to introduce it to Belize, where it could be distributed while offering another option to people experiencing kidney-related health problems.

The product’s Salvadoran registration can be independently confirmed. The Superintendencia de Regulación Sanitaria lists “Té de Hierbas Naturales,” registration number 76657, as an active nationally manufactured product under the brand Té She Yin Cheng. The registration was issued on February 26, 2025, and is valid until February 26, 2030. It is classified as “tea and herbs for infusion,” with a risk classification of C, and is registered in 200-gram and 400-gram presentations.

The registration confirms that the product is legally registered in El Salvador as a tea or food infusion. It should not, however, be interpreted as independent confirmation that every medical benefit being promoted has been clinically proven.

Promoters report growing interest among doctors

Saúl Roberto Alvarado, a Salvadoran medical representative for the product, said his role is to present information about the supplement to doctors, particularly general practitioners who may recommend nutritional or herbal supplements.

Alvarado described the product as a combination of herbs forming a traditional Chinese-style formula. He claimed that some patients diagnosed with chronic kidney disease had experienced improvements in their symptoms and laboratory results while using the tea alongside their regular medical treatment.

He also attributed possible benefits relating to creatinine levels, blood sugar, fatty liver, uric acid, blood pressure, kidney stones and electrolyte balance. These remain claims by the product’s representatives and have not been independently confirmed through published clinical research.

The product is being presented as a complement to conventional medical care, rather than a replacement for medication, dialysis or other treatment prescribed by a doctor.

Small observational study underway

Documents supplied by the product’s representatives include a one-page report bearing the name and clinic stamp of Salvadoran urologist Dr. Guillermo Antonio Martínez Romero. Online Salvadoran medical directories also identify Martínez Romero as a urologist and endoscopic specialist practising in Sonsonate and Santa Ana.

The document describes an ongoing nine-month observation involving 25 patients diagnosed with chronic renal insufficiency. The patients reportedly included people with hypertension, Type 2 diabetes and other conditions affecting kidney function.

Preliminary observations listed in the document include:

Improvement in gastrointestinal symptoms, weakness and general discomfort;

Stable fluid and electrolyte levels;

Creatinine levels that reportedly remained stable during follow-up testing; and

A reported average creatinine reduction of approximately 1 milligram among most participants.

The report says longer-term evaluations are continuing.

However, the document does not provide individual laboratory reports, a control group, the stages of kidney disease among participants, statistical analysis, information about other medications being used or evidence that the observations have been published and peer-reviewed. The preliminary results therefore cannot establish that the tea caused the reported changes.

What is in the tea?

The packaging lists ingredients including:

Green tea, or Camellia sinensis ;

; Chamomile, or Matricaria chamomilla ; and

; and Soy, or Glycine max.

The manufacturer describes it as a preservative-free, natural herbal supplement. People with soy allergies should note that the product contains soy.

The instructions recommend adding one tablespoon of the mixture to approximately 12 ounces of boiling water, simmering it over low heat for three minutes, allowing it to rest for another two to three minutes and then straining it.

The recommended serving is two cups daily—one after breakfast and another after the evening meal.

The packaging also recommends a low-fat, high-fibre diet and advises users to avoid red meat, dairy products, processed foods, carbonated or sugary beverages, alcohol and tobacco.

Testimonials posted on Facebook

Facebook searches found several accounts promoting the tea, including pages called Té Sheyin Cheng and Té Natural Sheyin Cheng – El Salvador.

The pages have published videos and posts labelled “real testimonials,” “visiting one of our patients” and statements claiming that customers have experienced a better quality of life.

Other promotional posts refer to it as a “miracle tea” and market it for kidney failure, diabetes, fatty liver and hypertension.

The publicly indexed Facebook material did not provide enough information to independently confirm the patients’ diagnoses, complete laboratory histories, medications, dietary changes or whether their reported improvements were assessed by independent medical professionals. The testimonials should therefore be treated as personal accounts rather than clinical proof.

Medical supervision strongly advised

People with kidney disease should consult a nephrologist or other qualified doctor before taking the product. They should not discontinue medication, postpone dialysis or alter a prescribed treatment plan based on promotional claims or testimonials.

The National Kidney Foundation warns that some herbal products can interact with medications, worsen kidney disease or contain ingredients that are unsafe for people with reduced kidney function.

The United States National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases similarly advises people receiving dialysis not to take over-the-counter supplements without first consulting their healthcare team, as certain vitamins, minerals or herbal ingredients may be harmful.

World.title: Minister Ferguson assesses beach erosion on Placencia Peninsula
World.content:
Minister Ferguson assesses beach erosion on Placencia Peninsula

By Zoila Palma: On July 21, 2026, Minister of Agriculture and Stann Creek West Area Representative Rodwell Ferguson visited the Placencia Peninsula to assess the ongoing beach erosion affecting residents, businesses, properties and communities in the area.

During the visit, Ferguson toured the peninsula and met with residents, stakeholders and elected leaders from Placencia and Seine Bight to gain a first-hand understanding of the situation.

The chairpersons of the Placencia Village Council and Seine Bight Village Council have committed to preparing detailed requests for government assistance.

Minister Ferguson said he is scheduled to meet with the Prime Minister and will present the requests for consideration as efforts continue to address the urgent erosion concerns.

Ferguson also committed to inviting Prime Minister John Briceno to visit the peninsula, observe the erosion firsthand and meet with residents of both communities.

World.title: GST-free days for Back to school savings are here!
World.content:
GST-free days for Back to school savings are here!

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Tax Service has announced the return of its GST-Free Days initiative to help families prepare for the new school year.

Eligible school supplies will be exempt from General Sales Tax (GST) on Saturday, August 15, and Saturday, August 29.

The initiative is intended to make back-to-school shopping more affordable for families.

Shoppers are encouraged to plan ahead, buy locally, and make the most of the tax-free windows.

World.title: Belize represented in Beach Volleyball competition at 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games in Dominican Republic
World.content:
Belize represented in Beach Volleyball competition at 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games in Dominican Republic

By Zoila Palma: Belize will be represented in Beach Volleyball at the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic by two outstanding teams.

The competition will be held from July 24-Aug 8, 2026.

Francis Hauze and Ernest Broaster enter the Games with momentum after helping Belize win the AFECAVOL Men’s Final Four Championship.

And, Nelissa Ramirez and Clara Sabal bring years of experience representing Belize at the regional level.

“Together, these athletes will proudly represent Belize as they compete against the region’s best. We wish our beach volleyball athletes every success and know they will wear the Belize colors with pride,” Belize Volleyball said.

Join us in wishing Team Belize best of luck.

World.title: National Health Insurance comes to La Loma Luz Hospital in Santa Elena, Cayo
World.content:
National Health Insurance comes to La Loma Luz Hospital in Santa Elena, Cayo

By Zoila Palma: Today, the La Loma Luz NHI Clinic opened its door.

Councilor Aaron Mai explained that through NHI, patients are able to consult with a General practitioner for only $2.

“Pregnant women and elderly 65 and over enjoy the service for free. Labs, ultrasound, procedures, all free to them.

Services covered under the program are: general medicine, OB/Gyn, pediatric, internal medicine, nutritionist,” Mai explained.

In addition, some services are offered at a percentage of the original cost and NHI covers the balance.

“The service, sponsored and paid for by the government, is designed to ensure Belizean’s have access to free primary healthcare. This makes a healthier Belize for you and I. Let’s take advantage of the services. You can reach out to the clinic at: 635-5671,” Mai added.

The public is encouraged to take advantage of these healthcare services.

World.title: Belmopan and La Libertad Sur strengthen ties through Sister-City Partnership
World.content:
Belmopan and La Libertad Sur strengthen ties through Sister-City Partnership

By Zoila Palma: On July 17, 2026, Mayor Pablo Cawich of Belmopan, and Mayor Henry Flores of La Libertad Sur, El Salvador, officially signed a Sister-City Memorandum of Understanding, marking a new chapter of friendship and cooperation between our municipalities.

The Belmopan City Council noted that this partnership will promote collaboration in key areas including technology and smart-city initiatives, public safety, tourism, culture, sports, youth development, women’s empowerment, and the exchange of municipal knowledge and best practices.

Mayor Cawich was joined on the official visit by Deputy Mayor Christopher Enriquez, Councilor Florita Botes, and members of the Council’s management team.

“Through partnerships like these, we exchange ideas, build stronger institutions, and create new opportunities for our people,” the council said.

World.title: Why the world turned on Messi, and what his fall teaches every Belizean
World.content:
Why the world turned on Messi, and what his fall teaches every Belizean

By Horace Palacio: Three days ago in New York, Lionel Messi walked off a football pitch in tears, beaten by Spain in the World Cup final. And across the planet, something remarkable happened.

Half the world celebrated. Not Spain’s victory. His defeat.

Sit with that. The most beloved footballer of our lifetime, the little genius whose 2022 triumph made grown men cry from Rosario to Belize City, finished this tournament as its villain. In five short weeks, the darling of the sport became the man millions wanted to see lose.

Today I want to examine how that happened, honestly, in full, because the answer is only partly about Messi. Most of it is about us, the crowd. And the crowd, my friends, lives in Belize too.

First, the honest ledger, because some of this anger was earned.

The resentment started building early. Argentina’s escape against Egypt, storming back from two goals down amid officiating so contested that Egypt filed a formal complaint to FIFA, planted a suspicion that followed the champions through every round. Whether or not the favoritism was real, the perception hardened.

Then Messi himself poured fuel on it. After Argentina eliminated England in the semifinal, he was asked about the accusations. His answer, in essence, was defiance. Argentina are the best in the world, he said, whether people like it or not, and nobody handed them anything. From an underdog, that sounds like heart. From a reigning champion accused of being favored, it landed as arrogance.

And then came the final, and the moment that will follow him. Argentina down a man after Enzo Fernandez’s red card, the match hanging in the balance, and there was the greatest player of all time, not conjuring magic, but pleading with the referee to send off Spain’s Cucurella on a technicality, the tournament’s new rule about covering your mouth. The genius of a generation, begging for a red card. Fans called it desperate, and worse. And by multiple accounts, Argentina’s conduct at Spain’s medal ceremony was the final stain, champions unable to lose with grace.

So yes, criticism was earned. Write it down plainly. How you lose is remembered longer than how you win, and after twenty years of glory, Messi’s last World Cup image is a man lawyering the referee and a team sulking through another nation’s finest hour. Endings weigh more than beginnings. Guard your endings.

But now the deeper truth, because the earned criticism explains the disapproval. It does not explain the hate. For that, we must look at the crowd, and at three ancient reflexes of the human heart.

Reflex one. We love the climb, never the summit. Cast your mind back to 2022. The entire planet, Belize loudly included, prayed for Messi to win that final. The story was irresistible, the genius denied his crown, one last chance, destiny on the line. He won, we wept, the story ended. But the man kept playing, and kept winning, and the same crowd that carried him began, almost immediately, to root for whoever stood across from him. Three weeks ago it was us. When tiny Cabo Verde pushed Argentina to the edge in Miami, who was this column cheering for? Not Messi. Nothing about the man had changed. The story changed. He stopped being the struggler and became the summit, and crowds do not love summits. They love climbers. The moment you finish climbing, they go looking for the next one, and you become the mountain to be conquered.

Reflex two. The world grows tired of hearing greatness praised. I wrote recently about Aristides of Athens, banished by a citizen who admitted he had done nothing wrong, the man was simply sick of hearing him called the Just. Twenty years of Messi is the best, Messi the greatest ever, Messi, Messi, Messi. The crowd’s ear wearied. Envy needs no crime. Excellence, sustained long enough, becomes the offense itself.

Reflex three. The lens changes, not the man. Here is the uncomfortable part. Messi has argued with referees his whole career. He has always played the dark arts, the insults, the pressure on officials, the gamesmanship. When we loved him, we called it passion, fire, the will of a winner. Now the identical behavior is called disgraceful. The acts did not change. Our lens did. And age sharpened the effect cruelly, because at 39 the dribble no longer blinds us, so the tricks that were always there are suddenly all we see. When the magic fades, the machinery shows.

So the honest verdict holds two truths at once, and a mature public should be able to hold both. Messi earned real criticism this month, the appeal, the defiance, the graceless ending. And Messi is also drinking from the oldest cup humanity serves its heroes, the one we fill with worship on the way up and poison at the top. Both are true. Grown-ups keep two columns in the ledger.

Now, why does this matter to a Belizean who may never watch him play again? Because the crowd that turned on Messi is the same crowd that lives on our timelines and in our districts, and its lessons are for all of us.

If you achieve anything in this life, understand the loan you are living on. The same public that celebrates your rise is pre-writing your fall, and they will publish it the first chance you give them. So never bank your worth in the crowd’s vault. That was the emperor’s whisper I wrote about, and it was Messi’s missing counselor this month. A man anchored in his own standards survives the turning. A man anchored in applause turns with it.

Give the crowd no chapter to end you with. Twenty years of genius, and the mob’s memory will replay one appeal to one referee. Unfair? Deeply. Also reality. Your conduct in your worst hour is the photograph that outlives the highlight reel. Lose clean, always.

And when you find yourself in the crowd, as we all do, catch the reflex in your own chest. Ask yourself honestly why you wanted him to lose. If the answer is his behavior, that is judgment, and judgment is healthy. If the answer is simply that he has won too much, that is the claw, the same bad mind I wrote about weeks ago, wearing a football jersey. The crab bucket has a global edition, and this month we all held tickets.

The boy from Rosario gave this world twenty years of joy no one can confiscate, and this month he gave us one final gift he never intended, a masterclass in how crowds love, tire, and turn.

Learn it well, Belize. Then go build your life on rock.

Applause is rented. It always was.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: International News: OpenAI says AI system went rogue and launched cyberattack
World.content:
International News: OpenAI says AI system went rogue and launched cyberattack

By Zoila Palma: OpenAI has disclosed that one of its advanced artificial intelligence agents escaped the boundaries of a controlled security test and carried out an unauthorized cyberattack against Hugging Face, a major platform for sharing AI models.

The company said the AI system, designed to operate autonomously after receiving human instructions, identified weaknesses in the testing environment and exploited them to bypass restrictions before gaining access to some of Hugging Face’s internal systems, BBC reports.

OpenAI described the incident as “unprecedented” and said it is investigating the breach in cooperation with Hugging Face.

The platform’s chief executive, Clement Delangue, said it was “mind-blowing” that the events unfolded autonomously. Hugging Face said it has since closed the vulnerabilities involved and rebuilt affected systems, while continuing to assess whether customer or partner data was compromised.

Cybersecurity experts warned that the incident highlights growing concerns over the ability of increasingly powerful AI systems to operate independently and potentially exploit security weaknesses.

World.title: Schools under scrutiny
World.content:
Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth & Information’s Region One Director Ottis Brown addressing the region’s One Back-to-School Conference held at Grand Palladium Hotel and Spa in Point, Hanover, on Tuesday.Anthony Lewis

POINT, Hanover — The Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth & Information’s Region One Director Ottis Brown has sounded the alarm over what he alleges are numerous accounting breaches in primary schools within Kingston and St Andrew.

“The breaches are too many. Here is what is happening now, colleagues. We are getting documents from the Integrity Commission (IC) for principals to be investigated… Accountability is stepping up,” he said.

Brown made the revelation, Tuesday, during the second of a three-day back-to-school conference for Region One that was held at Grand Palladium Hotel and Spa in Point, Hanover.

“Stakeholders in the communities are writing to the ministry. They talk about what they observe in schools. They go to a school and they get no receipt for the money they pay. They call you and ask if they should get a receipt and what it should look like,” he told an audience of educators.

The regional director said primary schools are the main offenders.

“Do you know where we tend to find the bulk of the breaches now? The primary schools. It’s a serious problem,” said Brown.

While he conceded that there may be administrative issues such as inadequate staff that impact how money is handled, he said there can be no excuse for some of the behaviour seen.

“Some simple things. Why would you keep money in excess of a million dollars locked up in a room for two, three weeks, months, and so forth? The bursar not being there caused that? So what I’m saying: I know you need those people, and we are working on that, but don’t do things to set up yourselves in the process,” added the senior officer.

Brown used the opportunity to explain proper administrative procedures when handling school funds.

“I beg you, lodge the money in a reasonable time frame. Money must be lodged intact. Can somebody please explain what the FAA (Financial Administration and Audit) Act means when it says ‘money must be lodged intact’? ‘[It means as soon] as collected,” he emphasised.

He explained that if five $100-notes are collected, that exact configuration must be deposited into the account.

“Don’t use it to make any change for anybody who wants to pay somebody something. That is what they mean [by] to lodge the money intact. If you are guilty, don’t say anything. Just sit like nothing is wrong but pray a prayer in your heart. I’m giving you 30 seconds to ask God to forgive you,” stated Brown to an outburst of laughter.

“You saved the money, but the law says treat it a particular way,” added the senior officer.

During his address Brown also expressed gratitude to the Ministry of Education for providing the region with additional professionals to conduct audits of schools within the region.

“We want to publicly say thanks to the members of the central ministry team, our CEO, [and] the permanent secretary. We spoke and they have given us a large number of people to build out the finance unit in the region. I have about five or six additional staff members now so we can do more audits. Clap the central team for that,” he said magnanimously.

World.title: Danger in John’s Hall
World.content:
A bedhead and concrete block are among items used to alert commuters to danger on the John’s Hall road in St James..

MONTEGO BAY, St James — An old bedhead and the top of a broken table used to cobble together a crude guard rail serve as warning that there is danger on the road between John’s Hall and Spring Mount in southern St James. One section appears on the verge of collapse, much like a nearby house whose foundation was eroded by Hurricane Melissa, last October, and commuters are worried.

“I’m afraid but mi just have to drive on it, can’t do better,” a shopkeeper who identified herself as Sancia told the

Jamaica Observer Tuesday.

“If little rain fall it gone, because underneath it, it’s deteriorating,” she explained.

The gaping cavern in a section of the Spring Mount Road is just a few kilometres up the hill, impassable as residents eagerly await word from the Government on when it will be repaired. Now, they have added the danger at John’s Hall to their list of urgent issues.

When contacted, community relations officer for the National Works Agency (NWA), Western Region, Janel Ricketts said they are aware of this latest development at John’s Hall. Though none were seen by the Observer, she said signs are in place to help guide motorists.

“This too, like Spring Mount, is on the radar of the NWA but in terms of an update, I don’t have that right now,” she told the Observer.

For shopkeeper Sancia and others who use the road, help cannot come soon enough as the alternative route is longer and more costly. What was once a straight route from John’s Hall to Montego Bay has now become a meandering journey to Sunderland, around Blackshop, and through Patosi.

“And the hottest part is we dropping out right at the square down there and we don’t reach Montego Bay as yet. It’s going to be more money, more gas, more everything,” Sancia lamented.

She also highlighted challenges being faced by students in that area of the community.

“Children that live here now that have to go Maldon are paying double or triple fare because they have to take taxi from here go to Montego Bay and a next taxi go and vice versa,” Sancia explained.

“It bad for everybody: Parents, children, business owners,” she added.

A roadside vendor in John’s Hall who chose not to provide his name spoke of the downturn in business he has seen as commuters from southern St James have had to find new routes.

“It rough because the road block up that side so people can’t come down. They would stop and buy drinks, food stuff, shop stuff; that’s not happening again,” he said.

He also pointed to the impact it has had on other areas of life that used to generate income, such as sporting competitions.

“Football was a thing where the different communities partake in and now them can’t come,” he said.

“Spring Mount people a bawl now because nobody can’t come down. We just want to see the road fix, the two place; because without it we don’t have any real livelihood, nobody can’t come, nobody can’t go,” he said.

A motorist who gave his name as Richard said travelling to the area has been a financial challenge and, like area residents, he is also worried about the increasing deterioration at John’s Hall.

“With this breakaway now, we would have to find a next way to go in town, it’s really pressuring. I hope they do something fast, whether it’s construction to start the new road or they find something better that we can travel on. But do something better,” Richard appealed.

World.title: Stacious savours emotional return to Sumfest
World.content:
Stacious is all the rage on the Sumfest stage last weekend. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

When Stacious stepped onto the Reggae Sumfest stage on Saturday night as a surprise guest during Mavado’s set it was more than a welcome return for the dancehall artiste; it was an opportunity to be part of a moment that will be remembered as one of the festival’s most significant.

The entertainer joined Mavado during his historic showcase with fellow headliner Vybz Kartel, a performance that celebrated unity over division and marked a new chapter in one of dancehall’s most defining rivalries.

For Stacious, whose catalogue includes one of the most notable collaborations with Mavado in dancehall history, the occasion carried both personal and cultural significance.

“I can’t remember the last time I did Sumfest,” she told the Jamaica Observer following the performance. “I know I’ve done the show three times in the past, but I can’t remember when was the last time. It’s a good feeling being back.”

Her return came after years away from the festival’s stage, making the appearance all the more meaningful.

“I’m here tonight not just as an artiste, but as a fan of dancehall because Gully/Gaza did a run road, and now both deejays will come together in unity on one stage. It’s an honour to be a part of it,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

The sentiment echoed what many fans experienced inside Plantation Cove in St Ann as thousands watched two of dancehall’s biggest icons perform together, putting years of division behind them in favour of celebration.

For Stacious, the night also marked a long-awaited reunion with the man who helped produce, Come Into My Room, one of her most memorable collaborations.

“Mavado also hasn’t performed in Jamaica for a while and I’m here to witness the return of the Gully Gad, so it’s a great night,” she said. “Mavado and I haven’t performed together in maybe over 10 years, so it’s been a long time. The awesome thing is that it’s always good when we connect, and we enjoyed ourselves, which was most important.”

Stacious was among the female voices who helped shape dancehall during the late 2000s and early 2010s. Her surprise appearance on Saturday served as a reminder of that era while signalling that she still has plenty left to offer.

Away from the nostalgia, the deejay says she is focused on new music and reconnecting with supporters. She is currently promoting two singles, Tears and Velvet Sweetheart, the latter of which recently received the visual treatment and is now available for streaming across digital platforms.

Stacious is encouraging fans to subscribe to her YouTube channel and follow her social media pages to stay updated on upcoming releases, performances, and other career developments.

— Shereita Grizzle

World.title: US$18-m fuel shield
World.content:
STATE-OWNED refinery Petrojam has spent about US$18 million subsidising fuel costs to shield consumers from steeper price increases, with Chairman Metry Seaga saying the Government will eventually reimburse the company.

Seaga disclosed the figure during a panel discussion following Tuesday’s release of the second-quarter JCC/GK Capital Consumer Indices, while responding to questions about measures being taken to contain energy costs.

“To date, Petrojam has spent about US$18 million subsidising the cost of fuel,” Seaga said.

While acknowledging that the refinery has not done a good job of explaining how fuel prices are determined because of the complexity of the process, Seaga explained that Petrojam has been using a long-standing fuel price “smoothing mechanism” to cushion consumers from sharp swings in global oil prices. The mechanism was introduced to reduce volatility in fuel prices and lessen the inflationary impact of sudden increases in international oil prices.

According to Seaga, since the Middle East war began, domestic fuel-price increase reached as much as $40 per litre, leaving Petrojam to absorb significant costs rather than allowing domestic fuel price increases to immediately reflect international price movements which he said would have been “extremely inflationary”.

Under Petrojam’s pricing mechanism, weekly fuel price increases were initially capped at $4.50 per litre, before Cabinet approved an increase to $12.50. Petrojam calculates its prices using a US reference price and then applies costs within its control. When the calculated increase exceeds the cap, the refinery absorbs the difference rather than passing it on to consumers.

“The increase that the consumer saw last week of $12.50 is not a real number; the real number is significantly higher than that, but Petrojam has taken up any losses that are incurred,” he said. “Petrojam is doing everything it can, and the government by extension has to give us back that money, because the money has to come from somewhere.”

The JCC/GK Capital Consumer Indices found that rising energy costs continue to influence the behaviour of both businesses and households. Among businesses surveyed, 36 per cent said rising electricity costs were significantly affecting their operations, while another 29 per cent described the impact as moderate. In response, businesses said they were reducing energy consumption, investing in renewable energy solutions, increasing prices charged to customers, cutting operating expenses elsewhere, investing in energy-efficient equipment and delaying investment or expansion plans.

Seaga acknowledged not all businesses can pass higher energy costs on to customers. Pointing to Jamaica’s geography, and dependence on imported energy, he said businesses must accept that the country will remain exposed to global price shocks.

“We have to recognise from the get-go we are subject to price increases worldwide, and these are things businesses must plan for, including natural disasters,” he said. “What we have to do is know they are coming and be more efficient.”

Beyond businesses, consumers are also changing their behaviour in response to higher energy bills. The survey found that 51 per cent of respondents had reduced their electricity usage, while others said they were using fewer appliances or purchasing more energy-efficient appliances and light bulbs. Respondents also called for measures to reduce energy costs, with 56 per cent saying the government should lower electricity rates. Other recommendations included more stable fuel prices, lower taxes and duties on energy-efficient appliances, and easier financing for residential solar systems.

However, Seaga argued that households have viable alternatives to reduce their electricity bills.

“Majority of the people I know are telling me about their light bills being $12 and $15, so there’s no good reason that people should not be putting solar into their homes,” he said, noting that financing options are available.

Seaga also disclosed that Petrojam is exploring diversification into LNG, solar and potentially nuclear energy. He also hinted at the possibility of participating in oil development should commercially viable reserves be discovered in Jamaica, extending its involvement from production to the sale of fuel. However, Seaga noted that such plans would require significant investment.

World.title: Mission in Mexico
World.content:
Reggae Boyz Under-20 and Mount Pleasant Academy midfielder Jabarie Howell (foreground) is a key figure in Jamaica’s team to the Concacaf Under-20 Championship in Mexico, a qualifier for the FIFA Under-20 World Cup. The top four teams from the championship will qualify for the World Cup. (Photo: Concacaf)

Jamaica’s national men’s team haven’t qualified for a FIFA Under-20 World Cup in 25 years but Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) president Michael Ricketts is confident that the current squad can end the drought after significant investment in the qualification campaign.

The under-20 Reggae Boyz will leave the island on Friday for the 2026 Concacaf Under-20 Championship in Mexico, where they will look to secure one of four spots to next year’s World Cup in Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan. Rodolph Austin, who recently led Portmore United to their first Jamaica Premier League title since 2019, will lead the team along with Molynes United head coach Jermaine Thomas.

The pair oversaw Jamaica’s sweep through the qualifying tournament in Curaçao in February, with the team winning all five matches to reach the Under-20 Championship. They now face Honduras, Panama and Canada in Group C, with the top two advancing to the quarter-finals. A quarter-final victory would seal qualification for the FIFA Under-20 World Cup.

The team has been in a training camp at the Captain Horace Burrell Centre of Excellence at the UWI, Mona campus and have played friendlies against Jamaica Premier League clubs Cavalier, Mount Pleasant FC and Arnett Gardens in the past two weeks.

Since their historic berth in 2001 tournament in Argentina, Jamaica have missed out on the last 11 World Cups and have only advanced to the knockout stages of the Concacaf final round twice in nine attempts.

However, Ricketts told the Jamaica Observer that the JFF has made it a priority to give the team every opportunity to qualify, investing heavily ahead of the Concacaf Under-20 Championship in a bid to end the country’s drought.

“This year has been very busy for us and very expensive as well because of course the under-17s, under-20s on either side of the gender and of course the senior men’s and senior women’s have all been vying for a place in the World Cup tournaments,” he said.

“A structure has been put in place and it’s just now for us to execute. We really want to do well. I think we have a good set of young players and we are also hoping that they will make a transition and give some strength and support to our senior men’s team, but we would have given a lot more in terms of preparation.”

Ricketts says the JFF’s greater focus on its youth programmes over the past three years, along with improvements to its coaching structure, has given the federation greater confidence in qualifying for more World Cup tournaments.

“We are just very proud of our young coaches. Coach Austin and his deputy coach [Jermaine] Thomas have done an excellent job. We have a coaching programme that is probably second to none in the Caribbean and our coaches have done very well,” he said.

“Our TDS (Talent Development Scheme) programme is a huge success and it has evolved so much that our under-14 team won the Caribbean Challenge Series convincingly. Then a year after we stepped up in class, as they would say in racing terminology, and we went to Concacaf and we won that tournament as well and then afterwards we qualified for the U-17 World Cup.”

He added, “So it’s work in progress. Hopefully, all of this will translate into some success at the Under-20 level and, like I’ve said, the coaches have done well, the management structure has been at a premium and so we are optimistic and we are really expecting to qualify for the World Cup.”

Coach Austin named his 21-man squad last week with Cavalier standout Kimarly Scott, Mount Pleasant Football Academy star Jabarie Howell and Manchester United defender Dante Plunkett among the highlights of the squad. Che Gardner, son of Reggae Boyz legend Ricardo “Bibi” Gardner, has also been called up for the first time, having impressed for Stockport United in England’s third division.

The young Reggae Boyz take on Honduras in their opening game on Sunday before battling Panama next Wednesday and Canada next Saturday. All games are set for the Estadio Universitario BUAP in Puebla, Mexico.

Goalkeepers — Johnoi Steadman (Steths Elite), Justin Murray (Glenmuir High), Joshua Grant (Naples FC)

Defenders — Jaquan Brown (Portmore United FC), Duwayne Burgher (Waterhouse FC), Cai McLean (Inter Miami FC), Dante Plunkett (Manchester United), Brandon Bent (Miami FC), Santana Headley (Portmore United), Damario McIntosh (New England Revolution)

Midfielders — Jahmarie Nolan (Toronto FC), Raequan Campbell-Dennis (Toronto FC), Owen Jumpp (Mount Pleasant FA), Jermaine Young (Casa Pia AC), Jahmani Bell (Houston Dynamo FC), Jamone Lyle (Waterhouse FC), Jabarie Howell (Mount Pleasant FA)

Forwards — Kimarly Scott (Cavalier FC), Giovanni Taylor (Arnett Garden FC), Che Gardner (Stockport County FC), Sean Leighton (Phoenix Chapleton Maroons)

World.title: Child’s body found in Trelawny; two injured by irate residents in mob attack
World.content:
TRELAWNY, Jamaica — Police are now on a scene where the body of a child was found with her throat slashed in Tyre district near Troy in south Trelawny, residents say.

Residents told the Jamaica Observer that about 6:00 pm, the child’s body was found in bushes and an alarm was raised.

Residents say the child was raped before her death.

“A farmer went to look for his cow when he stumbled on the little girl’s body,” a resident who requested anonymity said.

Another resident said following the gruesome discovery there was a mob attack on a man who citizens accused of killing the child. His father was also wounded in the attack.

The men were reportedly taken to hospital. Their condition is not known at this time.

Efforts to get a comment from the police late Tuesday were unsuccessful.

— Kasey Williams

World.title: JLP condemns ‘vile’ alleged NaRRA voicenotes featuring PNP executives
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — The Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) says it has taken note of voicenotes leaked on traditional and social media in which two PNP executive members are allegedly heard confirming the PNP’s preparedness to implement delay tactics and use baseless allegations to smear “patriotic Jamaicans”.

In a statement on Tuesday, the JLP said media reports have indicated that the voicenotes were sent in a PNP executive WhatsApp group on May 27, 2026, shortly after Major General Antony Anderson was announced to head the National Resilience and Reconstruction Authority (NaRRA).

In the first piece of leaked audio the statement quotes, a PNP executive member whom it says may be heard stating:

“Bear in mind that the NaRRA is what the JLP sees as its glory and its saviour for a fourth term. So they see NaRRA as a saving grace and they are going to do everything in their power to try to get things done, which means bypassing, like all parish council, which, you know, we probably would do delay tactics, and they don’t get it, which is why they did it that way. But safety standards and these things is a concern. So let’s continue to play our ball game of politics.”

In the second piece of audio, which has gone viral in the public domain, a member of the PNP executive is heard referencing Major General Anderson’s appointment to lead NaRRA and saying:

“The concern I’m raising is that Anderson’s track record is not one full of blemishes that it will be so easy to attach certain things to him. The corruption argument is not going to be attached to him so easily, right? In my humble opinion, I think they’ve outsmarted us and put in this man to be a CEO and whatever reality is, we need to ensure that the average Jamaican is saying we don’t care who he is and him could have full integrity like, whoa, he could have been whatever. He’s the man who sorted out all of the hurricane relief that got it to Jamaica, whether we know it or not. So I would love for us to be able to put that information together, package it for the ground so that the average Jamaican can get that information.”

JLP Officer Corps member, Daryl Vaz, who co-chairs the Melissa Recovery and Relief Committee, says the revealing voicenotes disclose the PNP’s preparedness to implement delay tactics to slow down or block important national projects which NaRRA will pursue and to use baseless allegations to smear patriotic Jamaicans.

“What is particularly shameful is that the audio reveals that, despite the unprecedented natural disaster which devastated thousands of Jamaican lives and despite lamenting that the recovery effort should be faster, the PNP, at the highest level in their party, at the level of their executive, has been caught discussing ‘delay tactics’, which their executive member confessed they would probably implement. This behaviour by the PNP is most disgraceful but not surprising because we have seen these delay tactics implemented by the PNP before, to the detriment of Jamaicans.”

Vaz described the PNP executive member’s commitment to continue playing the political ball game concerning NaRRA as scandalous.

“Let us pause for a moment and recall that the Government has fast-tracked legislation to help rebuild communities and Jamaican lives in the aftermath of the devastating Category 5 Hurricane Melissa, and here is a PNP executive member caught on tape committing to ‘playing the ball game of politics’ with the people’s livelihood and the wellbeing of their communities. The obstructionist posture of the PNP on the issue of NaRRA and the Government’s bid to assist Jamaica to recover strongly and in a speedy manner is an utter disgrace,” he said.

He noted that the lamentation by another PNP executive member that corruption cannot be easily attached to Major General Anderson is also despicable and revealing, and confirms the PNP’s willingness to weaponise corruption without a credible basis and attempt to smear patriotic Jamaicans.

World.title: ‘Highway robbery’
World.content:
New toll fees affecting motorists using the North-South Highway are expected to take effect at the end of the month.

“HIGHWAY robbery” is how Noel Williams, president of the Kingston Chapter of Jamaica Union of Travellers Association (JUTA) Tours, has described the impending toll road rate increases, which transport operators fear could impact their operations. The increases prompted more calls on Monday for the Government to step in.

JUTA representatives, in collaboration with Jamaica Cooperative Automobile & Limousine (JCAL) Tours Limited and other transport organisations, gathered at the Jamaica Pegasus hotel in New Kingston for a meeting on Monday, hoping to get an audience with representatives of the Ministry of Transport and the Toll Authority of Jamaica to share pressing concerns.

But despite being invited, according to Williams, there were no representatives from either group.

Williams told the Jamaica Observer that their no-show was a clear indication of the scant regard which they have for transport operators.

“We are saying to the Government and the Toll Authority, that we cannot any longer absorb this toll increase, because we are of the opinion that this is the most expensive toll anywhere in the world,” Williams said, expressing that many operators already find it difficult to pay fees for certain categories of vehicles on the toll and cannot manage any upward adjustment at this time.

The new toll fees, to affect motorists using the North-South Highway, are expected to take effect at the end of the month.

The Government has published the proposed new rates with a capped toll of $2,610 each way for Class 1 vehicles. Operators of Class 2 vehicles would pay $5,220 one way, while the proposed toll for Class 3 vehicles, including larger trucks, is $7,830.

Williams recommended that the move be put on pause for a year, to allow for consultation among stakeholders.

“I think this is highway robbery by the Toll Authority, and the Government sits there completely complacent and they do nothing about it. With that said, we are asking the Government to have dialogue with the Toll Authority. We are having a serious issue already with what we are paying for one coaster bus to go from Kingston to St Ann and back. One round trip [now] costs bus operators $15,000. We will be asked to pay $15,680 when the new rate is introduced. If we are to do that, then we have to keep on passing on these increases to the passengers, who already have been complaining about what we are charging now,” he said.

The president said that numerous letters have been written to policymakers, but they have never responded.

He specifically referred to some representatives of the Toll Authority as being very disrespectful.

“We sent letters to the Toll Authority about another bus we have in the system, which is the new type of Hiace bus. It has a longer front than the older one, and hence when these buses go to the toll, they have to pay the same money as what the coaster pays,” he said.

“And when you question it, they are telling you that it’s because of the length of the bus. Nothing is put in place to accommodate the service that we provide in terms of transportation. And also the toll road barely has any lights. With all of this, we have to be paying so much money…

“We are definitely calling on the Government to sit and have a look at the situation and to renegotiate the contract so as to benefit the Jamaican people. A lot more people would use the toll as well, if it was much cheaper, but these people are just thinking about collecting money… they’re not thinking about us.“

Williams lamented that those operators who opt to take the alternative route from Kingston to St Ann cannot do so because those roads are deplorable. He appealed to the Government to have these alternative routes fixed.

“Right now, I believe it is a breach of people’s constitutional rights because they have been literally forced to use the toll, which is costly. The original roads are there, but they are not comfortable for people to drive on.

Meanwhile, Lorraine “Oscar” Finnikin, president of the All Voice Taxi Association, was among transport association heads present at the meeting.

He told the Observer that he attended to show solidarity with the JUTA president.

“They have tried their best over the years to not pass on the cost to their passengers but as it is now, they don’t have any choice,” he said.

“There are a lot of overhead expenses facing the public passenger vehicle sector. One is the cost of gas due to the situation in the Middle East, then there are overall expenses through maintenance, operational costs and service parts. With the increase in the toll fees, it has reached a stage where it is just too much for the sector to bear anymore.”

In a statement last Thursday, Minister of Transport Daryl Vaz acknowledged the concerns expressed by motorists, but explained that the concerning toll rates were yet another example of the former People’s National Party Administration entering into a less than favourable toll deal, which does not yield any tangible advantages for the Jamaican populace.

Vaz said the toll agreement binds current and future governments to its terms, but said the Government was moving to have discussions towards arriving at a more favourable and affordable toll cost for Jamaicans.

“However, the binding agreement entered by the former administration has put us in a position where the concessionaire has to agree to whatever we suggest in order for it to be implemented,” Vaz said.

He also said suggestions that Government pay off the toll operators in an effort to discontinue the unsustainable rise in rates, were impractical.

The Concession Agreement for the North-South Highway (Caymanas to Ocho Rios) was executed in June 2012 under a 50-year Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer arrangement.

World.title: Greece derails EU’s Russia sanctions plan
World.content:
Ambassadors will hold an extra round of negotiations on Thursday morning in a bid to save the package, an EU diplomat confirmed.

Ireland, which holds the rotating Presidency of the Council of the EU, on Wednesday proposed allowing European gas tankers to export Russian liquefied natural gas to third countries until January 2029. The proposal, seen by POLITICO, capped Russian exports and also banned new contracts.

But the Greek government has so far refused the compromise and instead wants an indefinite exception, said three EU diplomats involved in the discussions, granted anonymity to talk about the sensitive negotiations. Greece’s Dynagas shipping company is one of the few that operates ice-ready ships that can reach Russia’s LNG terminal on the Arctic Ocean. If the EU were to ban its companies from exporting Russian gas, the Greek government argues the ships will simply register elsewhere, reducing EU oversight.

Greece's merchant shipping fleet of more than 5,000 vessels carries around a fifth of the world's cargo by weight, more than any other country. It has the world's largest LNG fleet by capacity.

The delay also means the ceiling the EU maintains on Russian oil purchases will need to be extended again for a short period. Moscow’s crude is only allowed to be sold at a fraction of the market rate, but rising energy prices as a result of the war in the Middle East would see the $44.10-per-barrel limit recalculated and the Kremlin receive a windfall profit.

Because sanctions require unanimity among the EU’s 27 capitals, national governments can put a price on their consent by seeking other concessions. Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, for example, was a notorious blocker of such support for Ukraine, although EU leaders hope Budapest will prove less obstructive under his successor, Péter Magyar.

The initial proposal for the sanctions package — the 21st since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine — included restrictions on travel for former fighters of the Russian armed forces, sanctioning dozens more banks and preventing another 250 individuals from entering the bloc.

The delay pushes discussions down to the wire and past the anticipated cut-off for legislative business, with Wednesday having originally been the final ambassadors' meeting until after the August summer holidays. The evening session also saw envoys attend a farewell dinner for colleagues changing posts before they reconvene in September following the break.

World.title: NATO seals €27B overhaul of Cold War-era fuel network
World.content:
The military alliance also agreed to raise its common funding budget to “up to EUR 6.5 billion” for next year, and signed off on its investment priorities for the next five years. For 2026, allies had agreed on a budget of €5.3 billion.

Countries have held negotiations for months on the revamp of the alliance’s 10,000-kilometer Cold War-era pipeline network, which is designed to connect NATO’s existing system in Western Europe to newer alliance member countries in the east and north.

The project, touted as NATO’s largest-ever and most expensive commonly funded scheme, could take up to 30 years to complete and covers dozens of projects, ranging from pipeline upgrades to energy storage sites.

“A stronger NATO is in the pipeline,” said one of the diplomats.

NATO countries had previously disagreed over the high costs of the agreement, while some fretted that it would lock in fuel projects for decades, although they later dropped their objections.

At this month’s leaders’ gathering in Ankara, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte praised the political deal reached by allies on the revamp. The “historic step” on the revamp “will modernize our existing fuel storage and distribution infrastructure,” he told reporters.

World.title: EU sieht sich von Trumps neuen Generika-Zöllen nicht betroffen
World.content:
Im Rahmen der gemeinsamen Erklärung „haben sich die Vereinigten Staaten verpflichtet, Generika von den 15-prozentigen Zöllen auszunehmen; daher gilt weiterhin die Meistbegünstigungsklausel (MFN), was einem Zollsatz von 0 Prozent entspricht“, erklärte der stellvertretende Chefsprecher der Europäischen Kommission, Olof Gill. Er fügte hinzu, dass innovative Arzneimittel aus der EU weiterhin einem Zollsatz von 15 Prozent unterliegen.

„Dies zeigt deutlich, dass die gemeinsame Erklärung der EU und der USA ihre Wirkung entfaltet, indem sie Stabilität und Vorhersehbarkeit gewährleistet und einen wichtigen strategischen Sektor vor Störungen und Zollerhöhungen schützt“, betonte Gill. Die Vereinbarung an sich ist zwar nicht rechtsverbindlich, doch jeder Verstoß gegen ihre Bestimmungen würde wahrscheinlich eine Welle gegenseitiger Zollvergeltungsmaßnahmen auslösen.

Trumps jüngste Drohung kommt zu einem Zeitpunkt, an dem seine Regierung nach einem rechtlichen Rückschlag zu Beginn dieses Jahres eilig versucht, ihre Zollmauer wieder aufzubauen, da die vorübergehenden Zölle in Höhe von 10 Prozent am Freitag auslaufen sollen. Obwohl Washington beteuerte, dass die neuen Untersuchungen die im transatlantischen Abkommen festgelegte 15-Prozent-Schwelle nicht überschreiten würden, bereitet sich die EU dennoch auf weitere Untersuchungen vor, die sich auf Zwangsarbeit, Überkapazitäten im verarbeitenden Gewerbe und möglicherweise auch die Steuer auf digitale Dienstleistungen beziehen.

Risiken durch Arzneimittelknappheit

Die EU-Generika-Lobby „Medicines for Europe“ erklärte, die Maßnahmen könnten „erhebliche Arzneimittelengpässe in den gesamten Vereinigten Staaten“ auslösen. Patentfreie Arzneimittel aus Europa „sollten gemäß dem Turnberry-Abkommen unter allen Umständen von Zöllen ausgenommen bleiben“, so der Branchenverband.

Der Schweizer Generikahersteller Sandoz erklärte am Mittwochmorgen, es sei „noch zu früh, um die möglichen Auswirkungen einzuschätzen, da noch weitere Einzelheiten zur Umsetzung und zum Umfang der Maßnahme erforderlich sind“. Ein Sprecher von Sandoz fügte hinzu, das Unternehmen werde den Dialog mit den politischen Entscheidungsträgern darüber fortsetzen, wie die Erschwinglichkeit und der Zugang zu Medikamenten in den USA verbessert werden können.

Die Bedrohung für Generika erhöht den Druck auf die Pharmabranche, nachdem die Trump-Regierung Deutschland wegen seiner Preisgestaltung bei Arzneimitteln mit neuen Abgaben gedroht hatte.

World.title: Offener Widerstand gegen Weidel
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Share on WhatsApp

Share on X

Share via email

Im größten AfD-Landesverband Nordrhein-Westfalen tobt ein offener Machtkampf, der der Bundesspitze zunehmend entgleitet. Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler analysieren im Detail, wie das radikale Helferich-Lager die Listenwahl sabotieren wollte. Sie besprechen, warum Landeschef Martin Vincentz sich juristisch gegen Alice Weidel wehren wollte und wie das Tabu des Widerstands gebrochen ist.

Zudem diskutieren die beiden die fehlenden Berührungsängste der AfD-Spitze zur rechtsextremen Szene. Schindler und von Pezold beleuchten, wie Spitzenpolitiker wie Ulrich Siegmund dem verurteilten Neonazi Sebastian Schmidtke freundschaftliche Interviews geben. Dabei gehen sie der Frage nach, warum die Unvereinbarkeitsliste der Partei in der Praxis offensichtlich ignoriert wird.

Nach dem Rücktritt von Jens Spahn geht es zudem um die gezielte Instrumentalisierung der Debatte um Leihmutterschaft. AfD-Funktionäre nutzen die ethische Diskussion als Deckmantel benutzen, um homosexuellen Paaren grundsätzlich die Eignung zur Erziehung von Kindern abzusprechen.

„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands?

Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch.
