World.title: 'Unheard and uncared for': Children in state care exploited by adults
World.content:
Zoey* has been missing for days, but there are plenty of adults who know exactly where she is.

The 14-year-old left residential care and is sleeping on mattresses on the floor of "trap houses", strung out on drugs with other kids.

Warning: This story contains discussion of suicide and descriptions of abuse.

The ABC has spoken with experts, advocates and residential care workers as part of a 19-month investigation into the sexual exploitation of children in state care.

It's an issue that Queensland's child commissioner Luke Twyford says would "shock" Australians, if they truly knew how "endemic" the problem is.

Zoey's shy smile flashes on the nightly news. Police say they hold serious concerns for her welfare.

In Queensland's child protection system, Zoey had 26 placements, including 14 residential care homes and seven foster care families. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

She and other children watch on as adults share needles during drunken parties.

Dirty sheets cover the windows, holes are punched into graffiti-covered walls, and syringes are strewn across the floor.

Zoey says she stayed at several of these party houses over the years.

"They got us hooked on drugs, so we'd keep coming back," Zoey said.

"We'd be off our faces — bad things would happen during those parties."

A trap house is slang for a home where illegal drugs are used and sold. Experts say vulnerable children are being lured to these environments and preyed upon under the guise of parties.

At the time, her guardian was the Queensland government.

She had been staying in residential — or resi — care, where young people live with other children in houses supervised by workers.

Zoey had her first contact with the child safety system at four weeks old. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

But she felt "unsafe, unheard and uncared for" in those homes, so she left.

"The state was my parent, but it didn't act like one," she said.

Hearing from those with experience of the system is rare. Now aged 18, Zoey says she contacted the ABC to expose what she sees as systemic failures.

"In every suburb, there's at least one trap house; it's kind of hiding in plain sight.

"That's what I want people to know."

Into the system as a baby

Zoey has experienced more trauma in her young life than most adults ever will. She knows Queensland's child protection system well. She bounced around it all her life.

During that time, she had 26 placements, including 14 residential care homes and seven different foster care families.

Zoey had her first contact with the child safety system at four weeks old.

Do you know more about this story or others like it? Contact Eden Gillespie at Gillespie.Eden@abc.net.au

at Gillespie.Eden@abc.net.au If your information is sensitive, you can also reach her at eden.gillespie96@proton.me

There was violence at home, and some adults in her life struggled with substance abuse and mental health concerns.

At the age of three, she was removed from her parents again when drug utensils were found in her nappy bag.

But instead of finding a stable home, she was placed in foster care where she was later "emotionally harmed".

A departmental letter, seen by the ABC, says Zoey was removed from one home at the age of 11 as the carers didn't meet the department's standards and there was "substantiated harm".

"It was reported that [Zoey's foster mother] was yelling, swearing, name-calling and using physical discipline," the letter says.

"It has been determined that [Zoey] has been emotionally harmed … in care."

Zoey also alleges that she was sexually abused by her foster father in that house, who is now deceased.

By age 12, Zoey had entered resicare. Soon after her first placement, she had her first suicide attempt.

She was in and out of hospital for several years, battling an eating disorder and poor mental health.

For a child who yearned for connection and stability, she says residential care was a cold and uncaring environment.

The department found there was "substantiated harm" to Zoey in two of those resi homes.

"Residential care is the most unsafe and inappropriate model of home care," Zoey said.

By age 14, Zoey and another child she met in care were sleeping rough; left to find refuge in laundromats, elevators, underground car parks, bus stops, shops and cemeteries.

Then, she says she was offered what appeared to be a lifeline: a place to stay with adults her friend already knew.

It was a trap house. She says she was handed a kitchen knife by a young woman and told it would stop her from getting raped.

A report Zoey received from the department when she aged out of care acknowledged that she was "spending time with unsafe adults" while she was away from placements.

For a child who yearned for connection and stability, Zoey says residential care was a cold and uncaring environment. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

It said she was engaging in at-risk behaviour "including alcohol and substance misuse" and had reported "experiencing harm, including physical assault, threats to harm and sexual abuse".

Sexual advances at trap houses

The ABC has seen a series of disturbing messages sent to Zoey by adult men who she claims had links with the trap houses.

In one message, a man, who Zoey alleges had sexually abused her, offers a place to stay and promises not to touch her.

In another message, a different man makes a sexual advance towards her, and she shuts him down.

Zoey says she remembers waking up in random places and not knowing how she got there, including in one trap house where she passed out after taking heavy drugs.

She alleges an older man attempted to convince her that he was her father while she was under the influence, and another woman made the children call her "mum".

At a different house, she says she feared for her life when she was left alone with a man who was drug-affected.

"He walked to my door and started dropping his pants. I made a run for it. I truly believe if I didn't leave, I would've been raped."

Children in care at greater risk

Advocates have long raised concerns that children who abscond from care are at a significant risk of exploitation.

A 2015 report from Victoria's children's commissioner said the "scale and risk" of abuse by "external predators" to vulnerable children in residential care was "alarming".

Principal Advisor on Child Sexual Exploitation at Integrated Family and Youth Service (IFYS), Conrad Townson, says trap houses are one tool perpetrators use to lure children into exploitation.

Conrad Townson says young people in residential care are often preyed upon. (Supplied: Project Paradigm)

"We've seen … young people invited to parties, coerced into sex with multiple individuals," Mr Townson said.

"In Queensland … young people have been … offered lifts home by these adults, and then trafficked as far north as Rockhampton, as far south as… Byron Bay and Coffs Harbour."

Young people in residential care are vulnerable, and this is exactly what perpetrators look to exploit, Mr Townson said.

"They may have a [family] history of domestic violence … of alcohol and drug use. A whole range of things can create those vulnerabilities," he said.

Genevieve Sinclair has worked in the youth sector for almost two decades. Based in Queensland's tropical far north, she says the Cairns region is facing an unprecedented increase in child sexual exploitation.

"It's at levels we haven't seen before," Ms Sinclair, the CEO of Youth Empowered Towards Independence, said.

CEO of Youth Empowered Towards Independence Genevieve Sinclair says the issue is rife in Cairns. (ABC Far North: Brendan Mounter)

As part of Operation Kalahari, 13 people in Cairns were charged with 301 offences against children after 54 youths came forward with allegations of grooming and exploitation since 2022.

But Ms Sinclair says there is "an immediate need for a national response".

"Often resources are directed towards policing young people. But child sexual exploitation is driving some key factors of youth crime," she said.

A Queensland Police Service (QPS) spokesperson urged anyone with information regarding sexual offending against a child to report the concerns to police and the Department of Child Safety.

A spokesperson for the child safety department said they could not legally comment on individual cases but said: "The safety and wellbeing of children and young people remains our highest priority".

"All children and young people deserve to be safe, nurtured and cared for and we would urge anyone with information regarding sexual offending against a child to report their concerns," they said.

Children in care have told harrowing stories. Now it’s up to the government to act The $20m inquiry is the fourth in almost three decades into what the Queensland government has described as a "broken" system.

Issue is 'endemic'

Residential care is often considered a last resort, but in Queensland, thousands of kids are being placed in these homes.

The Sunshine State has the highest number of children in resicare in Australia. As of February, 12,117 children are in the state government's care, with 2,388 of those kids placed in resicare.

A 10-month commission of inquiry into child safety published 52 recommendations in June to transform the sector, including moving away from residential care.

The state government is due to respond to the recommendations within the next month.

But Queensland's child commissioner Luke Twyford says the sector is in urgent need of reform.

Queensland Family and Child Commission Commissioner Luke Twyford. (Supplied)

He says it's "very clear" resicare "is not the best place for children … [and] that teenagers in our community are being exploited."

"We are still operating houses that would not be safe or chosen by so many of us, including myself, to place our own children into," Mr Twyford added.

As of last March, there were 780 children in out-of-home care who were self-placing, according to data from the Department of Child Safety.

"I think all Australians would be shocked at how endemic this is," Mr Twyford said.

"That there are houses in our suburbs where children are being preyed on, where people with ill intent engage these young people in drugs and alcohol."

Speaking to police was 'traumatic'

Zoey was a traumatised child trapped in survival mode. At trap houses, she alleges young people were encouraged to engage in criminal activity, including dropping off drugs and stealing cars.

"I put a tough act on, but behind closed doors, things were completely different," she says.

When Zoey finally recognised that she was a victim, she says she tried to report several of the houses to the police.

But she says "with [one trap house], they believed me but needed a lot more people to make a case".

Zoey says speaking to police was "traumatic" and that after that experience, she was reluctant to make further reports.

A report by the department, seen by the ABC, says "ongoing attempts were made" to support Zoey "to make statements to police to hold these people accountable".

"Police advice to Child Safety was that these matters could not be investigated due to [Zoey's] unwillingness to make a statement."

But Zoey said: "Why would I speak to police again? Why would I add extra trauma to my situation?"

A QPS spokesperson said it has dedicated child safety teams and its policies require officers to create a "child harm referral report… if they have serious concerns for a child's wellbeing."

A spokesperson for the Department of Child Safety said: "There will always be a need for residential care for some young people… and all attempts are made to limit placement moves."

They said that sometimes "a young person will refuse a placement offer and go to arrangements that are not approved".

Children in care 'deserve to be safe'

From police to schoolteachers and bus drivers, anyone who works for the state should be performing a parental role for kids like Zoey, Mr Twyford says.

He says it's up to all our frontline workers to be attuned to what children in the state's care are doing and who's engaging with them.

"When a child says that they didn't feel safe, we all need to listen and lean in and understand why they are saying that," Mr Twyford said.

"For too many children in our care system, we don't pay attention."

Now that she's aged out of care, Zoey hopes serious action will be taken to break the cycle.

Now that she’s aged out of care, Zoey hopes serious action will be taken to break the cycle. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

"What I went through was not okay, and what other kids in the system are going through is not okay."

" We deserve to be safe, and our concerns should be listened to. "

*Name has been changed

World.title: 'Grave concern' as Wagga Wagga's homeless threatened with $1,100 fines
World.content:
Homeless advocates are slamming the approach of a New South Wales council that has threatened to fine people sleeping rough.

Wagga Wagga City Council has warned homeless people living at a campground near the CBD they could face penalties of $1,100 or more if they do not leave the site by July 28.

Wagga Women's Health Centre president Vickie Burkinshaw said there should be a more humane approach to solving the crisis.

"Rather than treat it as a welfare issue, we're treating it as a compliance issue," she said.

The council says there will be penalties for those who don't leave the area before the deadline. (ABC Riverina)

The council's move comes two weeks after it issued compliance action notices for people at Wilks Park to move on.

That tactic was part of a NSW government-led response to the crisis following the death of an infant at a nearby camp.

Vickie Burksinshaw says the council is turning a welfare issue into a compliance issue. (ABC Riverina: Jess Scully)

But Ms Burkinshaw said the strategy failed "to understand the individual needs of the people they're claiming to support".

"Being moved on to another city without the wraparound supports, without the outreach, is setting people up for failure," she said.

Rachael Vorhauer, who has lived at the campground for more than three years, said the notices prompted her to leave Wagga Wagga and travel to Sydney in the hope of securing stable housing.

"I'm not in Wilks Park because I want to be," she said.

"It was a leap of faith to come to Sydney."

Rachael Vorhauer has been homeless for nine years, three of which she has spent living at Wilks Park. (ABC Riverina: Jess Scully)

The ABC understands Ms Vorhauer was offered accommodation in Wagga Wagga and Sydney.

She is now living in temporary accommodation in Sydney but her pathway to permanent housing is unclear.

Ms Vorhauer said she hoped there would be more support options in the city than in Wagga Wagga.

Homes NSW said there was no limit for how long someone could stay in temporary accommodation, as long as they were still engaging with their support plan.

NSW Housing and Homelessness Minister Rose Jackson previously told the ABC every homeless person camped in Wilks Park and Wagga Beach had been offered accommodation.

Homeless people living at a campground in Wagga Wagga have been warned they could face fines if they do not leave the site by the end of July. (ABC Riverina)

Fines could be an incentive, council says

Council general manager Peter Thompson said further enforcement action could be taken if people refused the support being offered.

"The knowledge that we will eventually exercise some form of regulatory power might incentivise them to take up the opportunities being provided to them," he said.

The council said in a statement that it sought extensive legal advice before issuing the notices, but could not provide any detail because the advice was subject to professional privilege.

Kira Levin acknowledges that councils are under pressure to act, but says punitive measures are not the answer. (Supplied: Homeless Persons’ Legal Service)

Homeless Persons' Legal Service principal solicitor Kira Levin said there were better ways to address homelessness.

"We have grave concerns about forcibly removing people," she said.

"We don't think fining people is going to result in anything positive. If anything, it will further marginalise people and move the problem."

Ms Levin said councils were under pressure, but argued individual support was more effective than "punitive measures".

She said temporary accommodation also failed to provide long-term certainty.

"If they do agree to leave and go into temporary accommodation, where do they go once their time is up?" Ms Levin said.

Ms Vorhauer hopes the move to Sydney will eventually lead to a stable home.

"I came down with a suitcase and, as it turns out, I'm still here," she said.

World.title: Trump administration accuses Chinese giant of stealing AI secrets
World.content:
TechnologyAI Trump administration accuses Chinese giant of stealing AI secrets Maggie Eastland July 23, 2026 — 6:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Trump administration has accused China’s Moonshot of improperly using US AI models and Nvidia chips to create the Kimi K3 system that stunned the tech industry last week with its advanced capabilities. The company “acquired GB300-equipped servers and has accessed GB300s in Thailand, likely to train its AI models,” White House Office of Science and Technology policy director Michael Kratsios said in a social media post, making the case that Moonshot violated US export control rules and companies’ terms of service to build its product. Moonshot co-founder Yang Zhilin. His company has been accused of violating US export control rules and companies’ terms of service to build its KImi product. Getty “Large-scale, covert industrial distillation aimed at stealing proprietary US technology and undermining American research is unacceptable,” Kratsios said. The semiconductor servers Kratsios referenced are part of the Blackwell generation of Nvidia products, which the US forbids from sale to Chinese companies. Though the Trump administration has allowed some sales of Nvidia’s H200 chips, it continues to prevent sales of the more advanced Blackwells.



Trump administration official Jacob Helberg, the Under Secretary for Economic Affairs, said Moonshot had carried out a “heist of invaluable American intellectual property”. Related Article AI OpenAI says its AI models went rogue and attacked a digital library “Lying, cheating and stealing is not innovation or ‘win-win’. It’s corrosive to productive economic activity and to the healthy economic development of nations,” he added. It comes after China’s Xi Jinping delivered a keynote speech to the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai, urging countries to seize the “rare, historic opportunity” of open-source AI while staking China’s claim to shaping the rules that govern it, and warning against new “historical injustices” from unequal access. A May memo affirmed that the US Bureau of Industry and Security, which is responsible for export controls on AI chips, restricts sale of advanced processors to Chinese companies outside of China. Trump officials are now looking into whether some companies took advantage of a loophole to ship advanced AI chips to subsidiaries of Chinese firms.



An Nvidia spokesperson earlier dismissed the idea of a loophole and said it has operated as though it does not exist. The company did not respond to a request for comment on the Kratsios post. View post on X Spokesperson Liu Chang of the Chinese embassy in Washington called Kratsios’ comments “entirely unfounded,” adding that China respects intellectual property protections. “Relevant individuals in the United States should respect the facts, discard prejudice and stop smearing and discrediting China’s achievements in the development of its artificial intelligence industry,” he said. Moonshot’s K3 upended assumptions that Chinese AI capabilities were meaningfully behind US leaders such as OpenAI and Anthropic. The Chinese lab said its open-weight model outperforms all rivals except for Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 on overall capability, setting off a rout in tech stocks similar to DeepSeek’s impact last year.



Moonshot “developed a sophisticated internal platform to conduct large-scale distillation against US models,” Kratsios said, referencing a technique in which AI researchers use the outputs of a so-called teacher model to train a student model and replicate some of its capabilities. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent voiced similar distillation concerns, though not specific to Moonshot, about open-source Chinese AI companies engaging in what he called intellectual property theft to create AI models. Related Article AI Moon landing: Why this Chinese AI model rattled global sharemarkets “This administration supports open-source models, but what we do not support is IP theft. If we see, especially, that overseas models are stealing from our great companies, we have the ability to sanction them,” Bessent said on Fox Business. Bessent’s comments echoed growing accusations from OpenAI and Anthropic that their Chinese rivals have made systematic and unauthorised use of results from leading US models to develop a rival generation of chatbots at a fraction of the cost. Anthropic has previously accused Moonshot specifically of distilling its models. Moonshot has not responded to those allegations.



Anthropic public policy executive Sarah Heck said in a post on X that Chinese theft of US models “creates serious national security risks for the United States.” In April, the Trump administration vowed to take further steps to address the practice, known as adversarial distillation, including weighing steps to hold foreign actors accountable. Lawmakers in the House and the Senate have advanced legislation with similar aims of blacklisting or sanctioning Chinese firms found to be improperly distilling from US models. World.title: Chargrill Charlie’s is the little chook shop that could. It’s just not so little any more
World.content:
Chargrill Charlie’s came into the Craveable Brands stable in 2023. It sits alongside Red Rooster, Oporto and Chicken Treat.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On an early Thursday evening in June, Mosman Mayor Ann Marie Kimber slipped into her local Chargrill Charlie’s, the neighbourhood rotisserie chicken and takeaway shop, to bring home her usual fortnightly order: cauliflower cheese bake, sweet potato fries (“most delicious things in the world”), and a half-and-half salad mix. The food is still just as good as she remembers from when the outlet opened in the early 2010s. “It’s certainly stood the test of time and done very well,” says Kimber, who was visiting at the same time as this masthead. Chargrill Charlie’s has perfected the model of the local chicken shop. “It’s the sort of family-run establishment that it was 20 years ago, with that fresh quality food, and doesn’t feel like there are any corners being cut.” The Lower North Shore councillor wishes them every success, but also doesn’t want to be seen playing favourites within her local community. In any case, right next door is a Guzman y Gomez, and Fishbowl has just opened up around the corner. “There are other amazing and locally run takeaway restaurants, you know,” she says. “We want them all to be successful, and it’s not easy being a small business. “[Chargrill Charlie’s is] no longer a small family business, it’s a big corporate that’s running it. And sometimes there are small family businesses competing with that.”



Chargrill Charlie’s is the story of the little chicken shop that could. Established in Sydney’s coastal suburb of Coogee in 1989 by South African migrants Maon and Saul Sher, the brothers and their family took the pokey corner chicken takeout, perfected the model, and turned it into a drop-in destination for gourmet, home-style cooking that satisfied family gatherings with its small mountain ranges of salads, roast vegetables, slow-cooked meats, and a melange of other dinner dishes. Related Article Small business El Jannah’s cousin has entered Sydney’s chicken shop wars In terms of international reputation, the chicken chain also punches above its weight (the chair that Justin Bieber sat on when he came to visit the Mosman store can still be found if you flip over the right chair and find the date scrawled underneath). Chargrill Charlie’s spread across Sydney with 17 outlets and had cracked Melbourne with two by the time it was noticed and gobbled up in mid-2023 by Big Chicken, or fast-food franchise group Craveable Brands, which operates Oporto, Red Rooster and WA chain Chicken Treat. Beyond pockets of eastern and northern Sydney, the renown of Chargrill Charlie’s as a local institution wanes. Chief executive Scott Bradley, a former executive at Grill’d, is charged with juicing up Chargrill Charlie’s with the competence of corporate franchising (its app just relaunched, for instance) and weaving the Sydney-founded brand into the fabric of communities where there is no legacy to draw upon. Scott Bradley, a former executive from Grill’d, is Chargrill Charlie’s new CEO. Janie Barrett Every aspect of the operation, run as a family business for three decades, is being combed over in the name of consistency and efficiency. Food is washed, prepared, and cooked in store, which comes with bigger wage bills. The challenge is to become more streamlined – ordering just enough food, minimising waste – without cutting corners.



Bradley calls it a “menu optimisation project”. “We’re looking at everything from equipment to systems to processes to the way we order, to different suppliers, everything, as fresh eyes coming in,” he says. There are some compromises he won’t make: Chargrill Charlie’s will never move to a centralised kitchen, he vows. “We know that this model has to be really carefully monitored,” he says. “We pride ourselves on that product quality.” No Chargrill Charlie’s is identical to another. About four in five menu items are consistent across the chain; the remaining 20 per cent is left up to the operator’s discretion. (Coogee, for example, does free ice-creams on Thursday afternoons.) Outlets with franchisees or staff from Indian or Nepalese backgrounds might feature curries in their rotation more frequently. The trouble for head office is that it can’t see what each of the outlets is serving at any given time. “I don’t want to promote 80 per cent of the menu,” says Bradley. “I want to promote everything.” Chargrill Charlie’s, now at 30 stores, has for the most part grown deliberately slowly. Members of the Sher family worked in the business (and still do), opening new locations and hiring loyal staff who themselves became like family. “It was an unwritten rule. You had to work in a Charlie’s for two, three, four years to earn the right to maybe get your own restaurant,” says Bradley. He concedes that rule isn’t feasible any more. “But we do have really strict quality control about who the new franchisees are.” There is a ceiling to just how big the chicken chain can get. In the world of fast food, chicken (deep-fried, bite-sized, tenders, even for breakfast) is the hottest protein to be selling right now. Even Domino’s is offering five different ways to order a side of chicken to save its tepid pizza sales. Then there’s the rising popularity of Korean fried chicken and the ever-growing number of air fryer-friendly options in the supermarket aisles.



Around the country, chicken chains are on the march: Lebanese charcoal chicken sensation El Jannah, one of Chargrill Charlie’s direct competitors, intends to run 200 restaurants, led by former Craveable chief Brett Houldin. In Sydney’s harbourside suburb of Rose Bay, where Chargrill Charlie’s has been for a decade, competitor and Portuguese favourite Frango had lines out the door while plenty of chairs and tables at Chargrill Charlie’s remained unoccupied at lunchtime on Tuesday. Chargrill Charlie’s in Rose Bay was quiet after Portuguese chicken chain Frango, which recently opened up across the road, brought new competition. Janie Barrett There are plenty jostling for supremacy in the chicken wars. “You’ve got [Chargrill Charlie’s], Nando’s, Frango, El Jannah, Ogalo ... You’ve got a lot of strong competition, all wanting the same sites,” says retail food consultant and Titanium Food director Suzee Brain. Frango Rose Bay, which opened in late May, had a queue of people outside. Janie Barrett About 80 per cent of the branded chicken market is swallowed up by KFC (817 outlets) and Red Rooster (325), she adds, and then there are nearly as many independent chicken shops as there are KFCs. “Australia runs into this [problem] all the time. We’re a duopoly,” Brain says. “To what scale can they scale?” A Chargrill Charlie’s outlet isn’t set up for the speed of traditional fast food. “We’ve got our food ready to rock and roll, you can just dump it out the window really quickly, but the challenge will be the ordering piece,” says Bradley. Brain says the ordering experience can be cumbersome.



Related Article Food & drink Not just raw fish: How Aussie sushi became a billion-dollar phenomenon “You’ve got to take your number, wait to be called, you’ve got to tell the cashier what you want, but then they only ring it up, and then you’ve got to go down to the counter and point at all the things you want in your pack with a different server, and everyone’s milling around because they’re waiting for their tickets, you’re bumping into the people that are trying to sit down and eat,” she says. “It’s a very clunky and uncomfortable experience.” Bradley isn’t interested in setting the bar too high. Sixty outlets is a more realistic number; maybe 100 one day. “I don’t see Chargrill Charlie’s having 500 restaurants because there’s probably not 500 locations where this brand would work,” he says. Those calling the shots are based abroad. Craveable Brands is owned by Hong Kong private equity firm PAG Capital and, after seven years of ownership, may be looking for an off-ramp for the investment, which is making less money. As a group, Craveable Brands isn’t growing: revenue dipped slightly to $226.8 million (down from $228.4 million the year before) and net profit plunged 21 per cent to $17.2 million in fiscal 2025, according to its latest financial report filed to the corporate regulator, which doesn’t give a full picture of its accounts. An $800 million deal to sell Craveable Group to a different Asian private equity firm fell over in early 2025 after Affinity Equity partners walked away. In September that year, PAG Capital co-head of private equity Lincoln Pan resigned as a Craveable company director, followed by then-Craveable group CEO Karen Bozic the following day.

World.title: ‘Russian Amazon’ hit by more massive Ukrainian strikes
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘Russian Amazon’ hit by more massive Ukrainian strikes David Crowe Updated July 23, 2026 — 5:31am ,first published 5:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Ukraine has launched new attacks on Russia’s largest online retailer, Wildberries, in a sign of its capacity to send explosive drones into enemy territory amid upheaval in the Ukrainian military after public protests about the war. The drones reached two of the retailer’s major warehouses in Krasnodar and Nevinnomyssk, in southern Russia to the east of Crimea, and led to flames shooting skyward in dramatic explosions that were caught on video and seen on social media. The attacks came at a fractious time in Ukraine after some members of the public gathered on the streets of Kyiv to express their concern after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky sacked the popular defence minister, Mykhailo Fedorov. Zelensky moved again this week to try to end disunity in the military by removing the country’s commander-in-chief, Oleksandr Syrskyi, a general who divided opinion because of concern at the mounting deaths among Ukrainian soldiers from his strategy of inflicting maximum casualties on Russia.



Zelensky chose Mykhailo Drapatyi, 43, to replace Syrskyi, 60, in the biggest shake-up of Ukraine’s military leadership since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. “It is important that all components of our Armed Forces continue to function in complete coordination,” the president said on X on Wednesday (about 7.30pm, AEST). Ukraine’s former military commander in chief, Oleksandr Syrskyi. Press Service Of The President Of Ukraine via AP The new military head of Ukraine’s Armed Forces, Mykhailo Drapatyi. Ukrainian Presidential Press Office via AP Fedorov was seen as a reformer who favoured a “drone first” approach to the war, relying on innovation and technology to minimise the deaths and casualties for Ukrainian volunteers at the front, leading to concern at his sudden removal.



The rise of Drapatyi to the top military post has won favour with some observers given his record of strong campaigns against Russian forces. In a video shared widely on social media, Ukrainians hailed Drapatyi as the commander of a tank that broke through enemy fortifications in Mariupol in 2014, a symbolic moment early in the war against Russian forces. View post on X Drapatyi said his plans included new operations behind enemy lines. “The President of Ukraine has set clear objectives for ​us: to continue and intensify offensive operations in all domains, to plan new operations behind enemy lines, to ⁠develop our military and its technologies, and to build up the capabilities of the Armed Forces of Ukraine,” he said on Facebook.



Wildberries head Tatyana Kim confirmed on Wednesday (Russia time) that the warehouses in Krasnodar and Nevinnomyssk had been attacked. Social media footage, verified by Reuters, showed a huge plume of smoke rising into the air in Krasnodar. Local authorities said one worker had been killed in another southern city, Armavir, when drone debris fell on one of the enterprises. Residents walk among debris following Russia’s missile attack in Kyiv on Sunday. AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky Krasnodar ​regional governor Veniamin Kondratiev said 10 people had been wounded in an attack on a storage complex. Drone debris has damaged two high-rise apartments in Krasnodar, where no one was injured. Authorities said a helicopter would be deployed to tackle the fire at the warehouse in Krasnodar. More than a hundred people have been engaged in efforts to combat the fire.



A strike by Ukrainian drones on Saturday killed eight workers, sparked fires and disrupted operations at Wildberries. “There are no words to describe all the feelings and emotions caused by the attacks on ordinary people, on our employees, on all of us who are simply doing our jobs,” Kim said in a post on the Telegram messaging app. Wildberries started as an online shop reselling apparel from European catalogues. It has since expanded its product range and evolved into a marketplace that includes third-party vendors. It did not comment on the scale of the damage. In a separate development, Russia is no longer willing to return some occupied territories to Ukraine as part of any deal to end the war and plans to retain them as buffer zones, according to people close to the Kremlin.



Russian President Vladimir Putin remains committed to taking full control of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region by force and would now retain areas of Sumy and Kharkiv regions near the border with Russia as buffer zones, three people said, asking not to be identified discussing sensitive issues. Putin had abandoned territorial concessions because Russia viewed increasingly confrontational statements from the US as evidence that informal understandings reached at his Alaska summit with US President Donald Trump had collapsed, the people said. Ukraine has stepped up strikes on Russia’s infrastructure, including oil refineries, described by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky as “long-range sanctions”. X With Reuters, Bloomberg Get a note direct from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: The 30 best movies to stream on Netflix right now
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The depths of winter demand a night in with a great movie. The problem? Choice paralysis. Every streaming platform has thousands of films available. To cut through that, here are 30 great hand-picked movies on Netflix right now. Don’t have Netflix? Check out our guides on Stan*, HBO Max and Amazon Prime Video. Atlantics (2019) A rightful Cannes Film Festival winner, Mati Diop’s spectral romance is about the many borders – emotional, physical and existential – that impact a young Senegalese woman and her partner after he attempts the risky journey to Europe before returning in a different form. Cargo (2017) One of the great zombie movies is a distinctly Australian production. Sherlock’s Martin Freeman plays the father trying to safeguard his daughter in an outback that has collapsed due to an apocalyptic virus. It is a taut, telling thriller.



Sophie Thatcher as Iris in Companion. Warner Bros. Companion (2025) A weekend away romcom swiftly transforms into a menacing AI-era thriller when Iris (Sophie Thatcher) learns harsh truths about both herself and boyfriend Josh (Jack Quaid). Controlling relationships find a new form in an alternately savage and bittersweet pursuit. Godzilla Minus One (2023) Japan’s Toho Studios took back the monster movie crown with this compelling new edition of a classic franchise. Set in a devastated Tokyo after World War II, with exceptional digital effects, this Godzilla astutely combines survivor guilt and atomic-era destruction. His Three Daughters (2023) A haunting New York chamber piece, this intimate drama follows a trio of estranged sisters – exceptionally played by Carrie Coon, Elizabeth Olsen and Natasha Lyonne – reunited for their father’s imminent passing. The emotional reckoning is vast.





The Invisible Man (2020) Australian screenwriter turned filmmaker Leigh Whannell delivered a horror home run with this nightmarish update of the classic H.G. Wells science-fiction tale. Elisabeth Moss’ heroine escapes an abusive relationship, only to realise her ex remains unseen but ever-present. KPop Demon Hunters (2025) Trust the kids on this one. Maggie Kang and Chris Appelhans’ animated musical fantasy about a K-pop girl group who have a Buffy-like knack for monster mayhem is a seamless mix of mythology, banging tunes and striking characters. Saoirse Ronan (left) as the caustic and judgmental 17-year-old and Laurie Metcalf as her mum in the film Lady Bird. AP Lady Bird (2017) Barbie’s Greta Gerwig announced herself as a director with this droll, heart-wrenching coming-of-age tale about where Saoirse Ronan’s high-schooler and Laurie Metcalf’s embattled mother trade blows. Deeply personal storytelling that is resoundingly universal.



Lady Chatterley’s Lover (2022) Almost a century after D.H. Lawrence’s sexually explicit novel about the affair between an aristocrat’s wife and a lowly gardener was widely banned, Laure de Clermont-Tonnerre’s resonant adaptation evocatively showcases Emma Corrin and Jack O’Connell. Late Night with the Devil tells the story of a talk show derailed by demonic possession. Late Night with the Devil (2023) Australian brothers Colin and Cameron Cairnes leapt up the sibling director rankings with this slow-burn supernatural freakout about a 1970s TV host (David Dastmalchian) whose occult-themed episode spins diabolically out of control. Long Legs (2024) Eerily perched on the edge of an unknowable abyss, this investigative thriller follows Maika Monroe’s FBI agent as a bloody series of murder-suicides becomes a creepy homecoming. The horror here has an oppressive weight. Then Nicolas Cage appears.

World.title: ‘There’s been dumb luck’: Patrick Brammall on Colin, Hollywood haters and what’s next
World.content:
Patrick Brammal with the Zak the dog, who is the eponymous star of Colin From Accounts.

As he prepares to wrap up hit comedy Colin From Accounts, the actor reveals why now is the right time to say goodbye.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s mid-April, and director Trent O’Donnell is on his lunch break from filming season three of Colin from Accounts at Sydney’s Centennial Park with the show’s stars and creators, Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer. “What embarrassing Patty stories do we have?” he wonders. There was that time Brammall was called “blandly handsome” by The New York Times (“wildly accurate,” says O’Donnell), or that time Brammall was mistaken for fellow actor Brendan Cowell (“Happens all the time,” says O’Donnell), but his favourite? That time Brammall was mistaken for Dyer’s dad. “Patty and Harry got off a plane at LAX [Los Angeles] and at the luggage carousel – Patrick went to the bathroom – and someone came up to Harriet and said, ‘Was your dad on [ABC drama] Glitch?’ “And Harriet said, ‘Yeah, he was.’ And they said, ‘I love that show, he’s so good.’ And Harriet said, ‘Thanks, I’ll let him know.’” Patrick Brammall as Gordon in Colin From Accounts. O’Donnell, who has worked with Brammall ever since he first directed him in A Moody Christmas in 2012, chuckles away before deciding to say something nice. “I’d be the first one to say terrible things about him, but he’s been pretty good. He’s still just someone who thinks in comedy all the time. He’s a very fun person to be around. He’s exactly how you would imagine him to be 99 per cent of the time.” Fast-forward three months, and Brammall is sitting at a cafe early one morning in Moore Park. He correctly judges I have yet to eat breakfast, after a hectic morning that also included discovering we had no bread in the house for my daughter’s lunch. “I’m a terrible prepper as well,” he says. “Harry’s like, ‘Write it down.’ She sent me a message as I was walking here this morning, and she said, ‘The hot plate was on, but I still love you anyway.’ And I said, ‘Thank you for not letting the hot plate come between us.’”



Related Article Sunday Life ‘A tear on my heart’: Colin from Accounts’ Harriet Dyer opens up on her biggest role He and Dyer are deep in the edit for the third and final season of their hit comedy, as well as juggling the care of their two young daughters, four-year-old Joni and 18-month-old Mabel. (For the record, Brammall, 50, does not look like he could be Dyer’s dad). “Look, there’s light at the end of the tunnel,” he says. “It’s very close to the end. We’ve been in that room for about 10 weeks, and we slowly go insane. We spend all day together in a dark room watching ourselves, which is not as fun as you might think, i.e. not really at all, and you go home together and parent the kids and then sleep next to each other. We are joined at the hip.” The pair have been married for five years and have been working on Colin From Accounts for roughly the same length of time. That they have decided to call time on the award-winning hit after three seasons is no great surprise – disappointing, sure – but the decision is deeply pragmatic. Harriet Dyer as Ash and Patrick Brammall as Gordon, with Zak the dog as Colin, in season three of Colin From Accounts. Patrick Brammall (middle) on set with director Trent O’Donnell (left) and actor Thomas Cocquerel, who plays David. “We’ve got two kids under five, so we can’t keep doing this,” he says. “Everybody wants us to keep doing more, and we’ll be sad because we love it. We love these characters. We love this world, all the ensemble characters and actors, but everything’s got to end, so let’s end it.”



Much like the first two seasons, season three is note-perfect: funny, awkward, emotional and deeply authentic. There are not many shows that have the audacity to start with a nipple flash and a disabled dog and then have you sobbing by the end of season two over the death of a parent while John Williamson’s True Blue plays in the background. Related Article Review What to stream this week: A hot new Aussie medical drama, plus five more picks “We never imagined a season two or season three when we wrote season one,” says Brammall. “We put it all out there, and we finished it the way we did, and it went well, obviously, and so we thought, what do we want to do? “I guess that’s why we left season two on a cliffhanger. We arrogantly assumed people would want more if we didn’t f--- up season two, and we didn’t. But I think it’s a really satisfying ending. I mean, Harry kept pitching an idea where I get killed – actually, no, didn’t get killed, just died – which was actually a pretty good idea, but it was just a bit too sad. “We know people’s relationship with this show is generally as a joyful place. And we thought, yeah, we like to pull the rug, but I think that’d be too much of a rug pull if we had Gordon die. So we didn’t do that. But [the end], it’s something we just felt like was a really nice moment thematically as well, tied to that first moment of season one.” Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer, the creators and stars of Colin From Accounts, in season one. The third and final season picks up in the aftermath of Gordon’s doomed proposal to Ashley. Without giving too much away, things have not gone well for the pair since we last saw them – Gordon on bent knee, Ashley begging him to stand up.



“And then we pick up from where they are, and it becomes clear the fallout from that, and what they had to overcome through that,” he says. “And some of the first few episodes is about going over the detail of exactly what happened and beyond that moment, and what comes next.” As for Brammall, what comes next is the big question, too. He has been That Guy on TV for 22 years, ever since he picked up his first role in Nine’s dramedy The Alice. Since then, he’s been a jerky older brother (A Moody Christmas), a good cop (Glitch), a comedy cop (No Activity), the love interest (Offspring), a stuck-up husband (Upper Middle Bogan) and an older brother who uses conditioner (Uncle Rad in Bluey). Kevin Moody (Danny Adcock) talks to Sean (Patrick Brammall), who is wearing an out-of-season crown of thorns for the nativity in A Moody Christmas. Patrick Brammall as Leo Taylor, Nina Proudman's third leading man on Offspring. Ten Patrick Brammall (back left) with the cast of Upper Middle Bogan. He is, in short, a fixture. “I was thinking about that the other day,” he says. “And I think it was TV Week that did a ‘Patrick Brammall through the years’ on Instagram, and I was like, ‘Thanks for the in memoriam’ … But I never have thought of myself as a fixture. But I am, undoubtedly, undeniably. That blows my mind that people might see me in that way, or people might see me as a celebrity … because I grew up thinking about famous people, and I’m not that. To some people, yeah, but not to everyone.



“I just mainly feel lucky, honestly, like really, truly fortunate. Obviously, I’ve done stuff right, but there’s been dumb luck involved, definitely, because I came up with a lot of people who are very talented, who haven’t been able to string it together in the same way. It’s very hard in this country to do it, and so I’ve definitely had luck.” Related Article ★ ★ ★ ★

Review Bond, James Bond? Not quite, but this Kiwi comedy is a delightfully dry spin on spy thrillers There is no doubt that Colin from Accounts has changed both Brammall and Dyer’s lives personally and professionally. Apart from picking up a bunch of Logie and AACTA awards here, they have secured rave reviews in the US and the UK, stole the show while presenting at the BAFTA awards in London, while Dyer won most outstanding performance in a comedy series at New York’s Gotham TV awards in 2024, where the show also won breakthrough comedy series. They have also both booked follow-up jobs - Dyer starred in the now-cancelled US comedy DMV, while Brammall starred in The Devil Wears Prada 2 earlier this year and will soon be seen in Apple TV’s thriller Last Seen (in which he stars opposite his doppelganger Cowell). “I was sitting in this emotional kind of river for 100 days,” says Brammall, who filmed the series over 100 days in Melbourne and Victoria’s high country. “I had to leave Harriet with Mabel [in LA] when she was 12 days old, and come back here … it was a crazy time to be doing a full drama about being a father missing his daughter.” Patrick Brammall in Last Seen, in which he plays a father whose daughter goes missing. The Devil Wears Prada 2, meanwhile, was an altogether different experience. Brammall was cast as Anne Hathaway’s “unproblematic heartthrob”, a big break in a big movie, but once the film was released, the hecklers piled on. “He’s Australian, he’s tedious, and apparently Anne Hathaway’s dazzlingly chic editor extraordinaire is in love with him?” one report opined. “Peter from the long-awaited new sequel is the film’s most egregious plothole.” Ouch.

World.title: ASX set to rise, Wall Street mixed; Oil continues to climb
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise, Wall Street mixed; Oil continues to climb Stan Choe July 23, 2026 — 5:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market is drifting in mixed trading, while oil prices climb another 3 per cent as fighting continues in the war with Iran. The S&P 500 slipped less than 0.1 per cent, coming off its best day in three weeks, after swinging between modest losses and gains for much of the day. The Dow Jones was up 61 points, or 0.1 per cent, in mid-afternoon trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.3 per cent lower. Wall Street swung between gains and losses throughout the session. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to climb, with futures pointing to a gain of 75 points, or 0.9 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.3 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.99¢. The majority of stocks in the S&P 500 rose after more companies reported strong profits for the spring. Expectations are high for the reports, and companies will need to match them after their stock prices already neared records on anticipation for them.



Philip Morris International rose 2.4 per cent after the seller of Marlboro cigarettes reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than expected. Its shipments of smoke-free products rose 7.5 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war The real oil shock from the Iran war might be just beginning Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist AT&T climbed 2.7 per cent after reporting a stronger profit than analysts expected. CEO John Stankey also said the telecom is accelerating plans to send roughly $US10 billion ($14.3 billion) to its shareholders this year through the buybacks of its stock. Super Micro Computer soared 21.1 per cent after the seller of AI servers said it expects to report stronger profit margins for the latest quarter than it had earlier forecast. It, though, also said that revenue will likely come in at the low end of its forecasted range of $US11 billion to $US12.5 billion. They helped offset a 7.9 per cent drop for GE Vernova, which reported a weaker profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected.



Alphabet ticked 0.1 per cent higher ahead of its earnings report, which is scheduled to arrive after trading ends for the day. Anticipation is high, and not just because the parent company of Google is one of the largest stocks on Wall Street. It’s also one of the biggest spenders on artificial-intelligence technology. Investors are looking for signs that the deluge of dollars going into processors, computer memory and other building blocks of the AI boom are producing the kinds of productivity and profits that would make the investments worth it. If that isn’t the case, stocks of chip companies and other AI winners would look very expensive following their rushes higher. Such worries have kept AI stocks at the center of Wall Street’s swings for weeks. Micron Technology swung between a loss of 3.6 per cent and a gain of 0.8 per cent Wednesday. That’s after it jumped 14.4 per cent in the first two days of this week to reclaim nearly all its 13.3 per cent plunge from the week before. It’s still up roughly 241 per cent for the year so far. Stocks broadly also felt pressure from continuing climbs for oil prices, which raise costs for most businesses and erode their profits.



The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 3.3 per cent to $US94 after briefly topping $US95 in the morning to touch its highest price in nearly six weeks. That’s up from less than $US72 early this month, which is roughly where it was before the war with Iran. Related Article Opinion

Media & marketing It’s News Corp v the ‘byte burglars’: Murdochs fire up in AI content battle Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Rising oil prices are threatening a reacceleration of inflation. That in turn could push the Federal Reserve and other central banks to raise interest rates, which would slow economies and undercut prices for stocks and other investments. The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.66 per cent from 4.63 per cent late Tuesday and from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran began. It’s already helped bring long-term US mortgage rates to their highest levels in nearly a year. Oil prices have climbed as fighting across the Middle East keeps oil tankers from using the Strait of Hormuz to exit the Persian Gulf. Normally, a fifth of all oil and natural gas traded passes through the narrow strait.



The auto club AAA said Wednesday that the average price for a gallon of regular gas in the US jumped again overnight to $US4.06. That’s still below highs of around $US4.56 per gallon in May, but it had been below $US3 before the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February. In stock markets abroad, indexes climbed in Europe following a mixed session in Asia. London’s FTSE 100 rose 1.2 per cent, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 1 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ‘That moment gave me perspective like nothing else’: The encounter that changed Lisa Gorman
World.content:
NationalGood Weekend ‘That moment gave me perspective like nothing else’: The encounter that changed Lisa Gorman Long before she started her eponymous fashion label or her more recent role as kikki.K creative director, the designer learnt a lesson that’s served her well in life. Jane Rocca July 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I meet Lisa Gorman inside kikki.K’s new retail store in Fitzroy, in the heart of Melbourne’s cosmopolitan inner north. A vintage workshop bench greets you on arrival – it feels more co-working space than retail – and it’s where they’ll host masterclasses, the first being a sketch series inspired by a calligraphy book that Gorman’s father gave her when she was eight years old. A cash register anchors the lifestyle and stationery brand’s space in a nod to preserve the past, while a moss-green cork floor screams of her love of ’80s decor. There’s a lived-in, homely feel here: a space where Gorman invites you to linger longer. Oh, and the green racks are the same shade as her Laminex kitchen at home, while oranges and browns in the retail space also show her allegiance to bygone eras. Kikki.K’s Lisa Gorman: “Heading up the rejuvenation of a known and existing brand nowadays requires a very different approach than what was required to start a label in the ’90s.” Peter Tarasiuk You’ll find journals, pens, and mix-and-match covers on display, but garments also feature throughout: pops of lemon-coloured denim, shrub-green jeans and hard-yakka blue tones are curated alongside boxy knits, shirts and jackets that show us Gorman the fashion designer, version 2.0, is back. Gorman has been kikki.K’s creative director for three years now and setting up shop on Gertrude Street is the latest move under her watch. It’s a role she came to after leaving her eponymous brand in 2021, her signature bright prints having established her as one of Australia’s most popular fashion designers.



During her tenure, Gorman has doubled down on kikki.K’s distinctive stationery, developed its travel accessories and introduced some fashion into the mix. Now, she’s hoping to tap into the love of neighbourhood shopping with kikki.K’s first foray into the high street – a notable shift from shopping centres, where the brand’s outlets have long resided. Gorman outside kikki.K’s first “high street” shop. Peter Tarasiuk Gorman has been instrumental in shaping the look and feel of the new retail space. Fitzroy is familiar stomping ground for Gorman, who has lived in the neighbourhood for 20 years with her husband, Dean Angelucci – a mid-century furniture dealer who owns a store around the corner on Smith Street – and their two daughters, now aged 17 and 20. Wearing a cinnamon jumpsuit that she designed (it’ll be available in-store from August), Gorman says the decision to join the high street was not accidental timing; there have been many discussions around how to grow a brand and introduce new fans at a time when brand loyalty is dwindling. “The focus on community and localised shopping is what we’re about,” says Gorman. “While shopping centres are a really important part of retail in Australia, and have been for the best part of 30 to 40 years, there’s a shift happening in the way people shop. Gertrude Street felt like the spot to move into and give this a go.



“Fitzroy is where I live, work and have traded over the years, so I understand the area and enjoy the product mix in this street. This felt really homely for us. It’s popular with locals and tourists, it has a mix of independent designer labels, such as from my best friend Megan Park to Northside Records; it’s a nostalgia trip for me. It’s a textured street that made sense to be part of.” Gorman (at right) with a model at the 2006 Australian Fashion Week. AAP Fashion has quietly found its place in kikki.K under Gorman, but it’s less about high volume; it feels more like the Benetton era of the 1980 and 1990s. “We’re not about putting out a new collection every four weeks and being stuck in the fashion cycle,” Gorman says. “That’s not useful anymore; people are focusing on building a wardrobe that lasts longer. “I’m inspired by nostalgic patterns, such as the classic bandanna or a simple plaid. I am also bringing coloured denim back. This reminds me of growing up in the ’80s. There are barrel jean shapes, cropped oversized denim jackets and patching – it’s an ode to the time that reminds me of my childhood.” Lisa Gorman has added colourful apparel to kikki.K’s range. “I’m inspired by nostalgic patterns,” she says. @kikki.k/Instagram



That childhood was spent in the Victorian coastal town of Warrnambool. Gorman is the eldest of four daughters, and she went on to become a nurse before becoming a fashion designer. She followed in the footsteps of her late father, Brian, who went back to TAFE to study English when she was in high school. (English was one of the requirements needed for him to become a nurse.) He had left school at 14 to go to work to help support his mum and siblings. Gorman’s maternal relatives worked at Warrnambool’s Fletcher Jones: her grandfather was the company’s accountant while her mother, Jane, and aunts all worked on the department’s shop floor. Fabric swatches became a part-time obsession; the warp and weft would inspire her own solo exhibition, Fluorescence, held at Warrnambool Art Gallery three years ago. Related Article Fashion designers The women who walked away from fashion to find something more As a child, Gorman loved sewing clothes for her Barbie dolls with her sisters. They’d fill Tupperware bowls with hand-sewn rah-rah (ruffled, tiered) skirts and boob-tube tops for their imaginary poolside Barbie runway shows. She also spent hours at the kitchen table tracing calligraphy. “I am still quite analogue myself,” Gorman says. “I don’t use the Adobe suite. I still sketch, and it goes back to my time as a kid when I just loved that feeling of drawing.”



Gorman arrived in Melbourne in the 1990s to start work as a nurse at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. One day, strolling through the city after work, wearing her nursing whites and dreaming about fashion, she stumbled upon a sign in the window of the Mariana Hardwick bridal store on Bourke Street. “They were looking for two trainees,” she says. “What drew me in was the sheer scale and architecture of the [wedding] dresses, and the hours, thought and hand-finishing touches put into those sculptural pieces. I walked in, had a good chat with Mariana and got the job.” Gorman ultimately left nursing, but says her experiences at the time have stayed with her. “When I was 18, I was looking after a terminally ill girl of the same age who was diagnosed with an aggressive cancer,” Gorman says. “One day, she asked me to cut off her long hair and I remember sitting at the end of her bed and thinking, this woman is my age – it didn’t feel right. It was really eye-opening for me. ‘I’ve never been the type of person to let go of opportunities, so saying yes to this job felt right.’ Lisa Gorman “It was the first time I’d ever cared for someone my age that had a life that was about to be shortened. That moment gave me perspective like nothing else and that has always stuck with me. What I saw and experienced gave me such a level head when it came to the fashion industry. It kept everything in perspective and served me well in life.”



Gorman is adamant that letter-writing is not dead, and neither is keeping a journal – they’re both part of the increasing appreciation for slowing down and finding the analogue element in an age of digital fatigue. “People are returning to writing things down, so there’s still 100 per cent a place for paper in our society,” says Gorman. “But the value around paper is changing and we’d be fools not to realise that. Related Article Australian fashion What Gorman did next: the designer weaving new patterns “In this digital age, a quality notebook and pen are viewed almost as luxury items. It’s the time, thought and permanency that stationery can provide that I feel is the luxury in paper these days, and without it carrying a luxury price tag – at least not at kikki.K. The value is in what it provides to you, rather than what it costs you to buy.” Despite coming from the era of Australian fashion that gave us high-octane labels such as Sass & Bide and Zimmermann, Gorman has always been an advocate for applying a more measured pace to work and life. In her 20s, a two-week visit to New York turned into a stay that lasted a few years while she took on a number of jobs. Meanwhile, she says kikki.K’s DNA, which lies in its heritage of quality stationery, is firmly staying put. She’s well versed in running a business, having done so for 21 years, and has quietly found her feet at the helm of kikki.K, which is celebrating 25 years of operation after being bought out from voluntary administration in 2020.

World.title: There’s one major flaw with new ‘business class’ day trip to a world wonder
World.content:
InspirationNew Zealand There’s one major flaw with new ‘business class’ day trip to a world wonder Natasha Bazika July 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Anyone who has ever flown business class knows the real luxury isn’t the wider seat or the gourmet meals (though they’re definitely perks). It’s the curtain, a visual barrier that separates you from the frantic, elbow-to-elbow situation of the main cabin. RealNZ and Altitude Tours have essentially pulled that velvet curtain across the day trip from Queenstown to Milford Sound with their new premium tour, Milford Sound Business Class. Milford Sound on the MV Sinbad. The upgrade starts at 7.30am. Instead of the typical 50-seat coach, I’m in a 14-seat Mercedes Sprinter. A lambswool blanket is left on my seat and a ginger tonic waits in the pocket, a preemptive strike against the notoriously winding roads ahead. Our driver, Ash, handles the two-hour stretch to Te Anau with a running commentary of fast facts. My favourite is the Maori legend of Lake Wakatipu, New Zealand’s longest lake, said to have been formed by the burning body of a giant taniwha named Matau. “Some say you can still see his heart beating with the rise and fall of the lake level,” she says over the microphone. “It pulses around 12 centimetres every half hour.”



By our morning tea stop in Te Anau, I’m entirely sold on the road experience. But the weight of the $NZ699 ($575) a person ticket rests on the cruise and the five-course tasting menu. To deliver it, they’ve partnered with chef Tom Hishon from Auckland’s acclaimed seafood restaurant, kingi, to bring the sensibility of a high-end urban restaurant and set it afloat in the middle of Fiordland. 



I sit down for a course, spot a waterfall spilling down the cliffs, and run to the top deck. I come down for the next dish, paua served in-shell with black garlic, only for the captain to steer us beneath Stirling Falls moments later for what she calls a “glacial facial”. Another few bites arrive, Mount Cook Alpine caviar served on a potato rosti with sour cream and a Titi (muttonbird) croquette with a delightful citrus spin. The menu is by chef Tom Hishon of the acclaimed Auckland restaurant kingi. For the main, we scoop up Fiordland wapiti (elk) tartare with potato crisps, and swallow in one bite smoked eel under a slice of beetroot. The windows at each table frame the landscape, but on this unusually bright day, they mostly reflect glare and streaks of salt. Besides, no one comes to Milford Sound to stare at it through a window. Someone shouts “dolphins!” at the bow, and every passenger clears out. No one comes back in a hurry, prompting the staff to bring dessert up instead, a flat white-inspired dish served in a glass.



The food is well executed, exactly what you would expect from Hishon, but the portions are too light for a 12-hour day. That becomes most obvious during the optional wine pairing, where generous pours arrive, two at a time, alongside one-bite courses. Related Article Opinion

Adventure holidays I went on my first big hike in my 40s. It changed the way I see travel Bianca O'Neill Contributor Drinking like that on an empty stomach before a three-hour drive back to Queenstown is a tough sell. For a faster return, you can skip the road and fly back by plane ($NZ500) or helicopter ($NZ1000), but that doesn’t fix the issue. There just isn’t quite enough food for the day. A more substantial main would have made a real difference here. Those of us who skip the scenic flight back load onto the van and find a packet of chips and a chocolate bar waiting on our seats. The crinkle of packets being opened and finished fills the van before we’ve even passed the edge of the national park. THE DETAILS



CRUISE

RealNZ Milford Sound Business Class starts from $NZ699 a person and includes return transfers from selected Queenstown accommodation, morning tea and coffee in Te Anau, a five-course tasting menu, and a two-hour Milford Sound cruise. Guests can upgrade to a scenic fixed-wing flight back from around $NZ500, or a helicopter flight with optional alpine landing from around $NZ1000, weather permitting. The optional wine pairing is $NZ65 a person, payable on the day. See realnz.com STAY

QT Queenstown (qthotels.com) has rooms from around $NZ450 a night. In Te Anau, Tasman Holiday Parks (tasmanholidayparks.com) has self-contained cabins, apartments and powered sites; one-bedroom apartments from around $NZ275 a night. See tasmanholidayparks.com; qthotels.com/queenstown FLY

Air New Zealand, Qantas and Virgin Australia operate direct flights from Brisbane, Sydney and Melbourne to Queenstown. HIRE CAR

Snap Rentals has a branch five minutes from Queenstown Airport with a free shuttle service. It’s also one of the few rental companies offering one-way hires, so you don’t need to return the car to Queenstown if you plan to drive elsewhere. See snaprentals.co.nz The writer travelled as a guest of Luxury New Zealand Collection. See luxurynewzealandcollection.com

World.title: Trump administration accuses Chinese giant of stealing AI secrets
World.content:
TechnologyAI Trump administration accuses Chinese giant of stealing AI secrets Maggie Eastland July 23, 2026 — 6:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Trump administration has accused China’s Moonshot of improperly using US AI models and Nvidia chips to create the Kimi K3 system that stunned the tech industry last week with its advanced capabilities. The company “acquired GB300-equipped servers and has accessed GB300s in Thailand, likely to train its AI models,” White House Office of Science and Technology policy director Michael Kratsios said in a social media post, making the case that Moonshot violated US export control rules and companies’ terms of service to build its product. Moonshot co-founder Yang Zhilin. His company has been accused of violating US export control rules and companies’ terms of service to build its KImi product. Getty “Large-scale, covert industrial distillation aimed at stealing proprietary US technology and undermining American research is unacceptable,” Kratsios said. The semiconductor servers Kratsios referenced are part of the Blackwell generation of Nvidia products, which the US forbids from sale to Chinese companies. Though the Trump administration has allowed some sales of Nvidia’s H200 chips, it continues to prevent sales of the more advanced Blackwells.



Trump administration official Jacob Helberg, the Under Secretary for Economic Affairs, said Moonshot had carried out a “heist of invaluable American intellectual property”. Related Article AI OpenAI says its AI models went rogue and attacked a digital library “Lying, cheating and stealing is not innovation or ‘win-win’. It’s corrosive to productive economic activity and to the healthy economic development of nations,” he added. It comes after China’s Xi Jinping delivered a keynote speech to the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai, urging countries to seize the “rare, historic opportunity” of open-source AI while staking China’s claim to shaping the rules that govern it, and warning against new “historical injustices” from unequal access. A May memo affirmed that the US Bureau of Industry and Security, which is responsible for export controls on AI chips, restricts sale of advanced processors to Chinese companies outside of China. Trump officials are now looking into whether some companies took advantage of a loophole to ship advanced AI chips to subsidiaries of Chinese firms.



An Nvidia spokesperson earlier dismissed the idea of a loophole and said it has operated as though it does not exist. The company did not respond to a request for comment on the Kratsios post. View post on X Spokesperson Liu Chang of the Chinese embassy in Washington called Kratsios’ comments “entirely unfounded,” adding that China respects intellectual property protections. “Relevant individuals in the United States should respect the facts, discard prejudice and stop smearing and discrediting China’s achievements in the development of its artificial intelligence industry,” he said. Moonshot’s K3 upended assumptions that Chinese AI capabilities were meaningfully behind US leaders such as OpenAI and Anthropic. The Chinese lab said its open-weight model outperforms all rivals except for Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 on overall capability, setting off a rout in tech stocks similar to DeepSeek’s impact last year.



Moonshot “developed a sophisticated internal platform to conduct large-scale distillation against US models,” Kratsios said, referencing a technique in which AI researchers use the outputs of a so-called teacher model to train a student model and replicate some of its capabilities. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent voiced similar distillation concerns, though not specific to Moonshot, about open-source Chinese AI companies engaging in what he called intellectual property theft to create AI models. Related Article AI Moon landing: Why this Chinese AI model rattled global sharemarkets “This administration supports open-source models, but what we do not support is IP theft. If we see, especially, that overseas models are stealing from our great companies, we have the ability to sanction them,” Bessent said on Fox Business. Bessent’s comments echoed growing accusations from OpenAI and Anthropic that their Chinese rivals have made systematic and unauthorised use of results from leading US models to develop a rival generation of chatbots at a fraction of the cost. Anthropic has previously accused Moonshot specifically of distilling its models. Moonshot has not responded to those allegations.



Anthropic public policy executive Sarah Heck said in a post on X that Chinese theft of US models “creates serious national security risks for the United States.” In April, the Trump administration vowed to take further steps to address the practice, known as adversarial distillation, including weighing steps to hold foreign actors accountable. Lawmakers in the House and the Senate have advanced legislation with similar aims of blacklisting or sanctioning Chinese firms found to be improperly distilling from US models.
